"WrrAT you please," means, in many cases, "I expect much more than I can in reason ask for." A BOY, when asked whit a "spectator" was, said that it was "a tater with a speck in it." A LITTLE four-year-old, on seeing a half-moon for the first time, exclaimed—" Oh, pa, the moon's broken I" LITTLE NELLIE was reading a lesson about ice to her grandmother. "Do you know what ice is, Nellie 7" "Yes, grandmamma, it's water fast asleep." "JoriN, you are not listening to a word I am saying 1" " Why, my dear, I am all ears." "I know you are, and that makes it all the more pro- voking." THE origin of the expression "rainiag cats and Islogs" is probably the same as "hailing omnibuses." SMITH :—" I say, Jones, can your wife cook?" Jones :---" Oh, yes, she can cook; the only trouble is that I can't eat what she cooks." JOANNA, in the kitchen, ivaxas angry with the chambermaid. ;t1 frigidly remarks—" If there is anything that I in, it is semtbody I don't like." JUDGE—" Prisoner at the bar, have you anything further to state in your defence 7" Prisoner—" No, niy lord; just deal with me as you would with your- self if you were in my place." "JOHNNY, I have discovered that you have taken more maple sugar than I gave yen." "Yes, grand- ma, I've been making believe there was another little boy spending the day with me." "SH E—" Why don't you dance?" He—" It tires me too much ; and, to tell the truth, I am rather fond of myself." She—" Ahl well, you need fear no rival." SAID a rather frivolous lady to a friend—" It may be years and years before I find my ideal man." And what are you going to do in the meantime 7" "Get married, I suppose." CLERK (to busy employer)—" There is a gentle- man outside, sir, who says that he is a very old friend of your father's." Busy employer—" Tell him I'm sorry, but my father is dead.' THERE is a girl who boasts of having a watch that keeps correct time. She was heard to remark not long ago, as she pulled it out, "If the sun isn't over the hill in a minute tad a half, he will be late."

A SHORT time since a disorderly Emeralcier faith- fully promised the magistrates of a certain burgh that, if they would lct him off, "ho would't be five minutes in the town after he was out of it !" A LITTLE girl defined fan to be "a thing to wipe warm off with." And a sturdy boy said that while he was eating he was happy, and when he had finished he was tight, so that must be appetite. A FORMER member for Dundalk was "heckled" about running a horse in a race on a Sunday. "Yes, the horse did run on a Sunday; but," said the can- didate trumphantly, "it won the race!" SHOPMAN in large linen drapery establishment calling boy: "Cash !" Countryman "Great turnips, can't you give me time to get my purse out? I don't want no credit, I don't! I'm going to pay you cash as soon as I can get at iii" A BRIGHT little boy, saying the Lord's Prayer one evening, when he came to the petition, "Give us this day our daily bread," paused a moment, then made the unauthorised addition, "With plenty of butter on it," and went on triumphantly to the final "amen." TRACKMAN (I 0 tramp)—" Sure yez had better get of the track, the fasht mail is due." Tramp—" Say boss, ger don't tink I'd let it run over me, do ye 7" "• Begorra, it isn't that I fear, but the engineer will take that nose of yez for a red light, and shtop the train."

"I Alr”going to buy a light coat to match these trousers, he remarked to his wife the other day, "and a light pair of gloves to match the coat, and a light soft hat to match--," "Your head, I sup- pose," interrupted the wife gently, and the house- hold knew no harmony that day. ME..NODDY—" Ah, Madam Do I have the pleasure of taking in mine the hand that has penned so much charming verse ? " Madam—" Poetry, sir —poetry; and I neter write with a pen, but always with a type writer l" THE Due de Morny's definition of a polite man is the hardest to realise of any ever given. "A polite man," said he, "is one who listen with interest to things he knows all about when they are told by a person who knows nothing about them." "AND now, sir," said the examiner, "pray tell me in which of his battles was the great Gustavus Adolphus killed?" After a considerable time spent in deep reflection the youth replied, "Well, sir, to the best of my belief he was killed in the last battle , he ever fought." AN Edinburgh dairyman was spoken to the other day by a customer for having rendered an account for milk with the entries twice charged. "Well," the dairyman replied. "I have asked at several con- tractors' lately, and they say everything is now dons by double entry." FONDMOTHER —" I admire Mr. Quillhootergreatly, Julia." Fond daughter—" Why, mother?" Fond mother—" He is such a splendid and successful busi- ness man." Fond daughter—" I don't think so. He has been visiting me for two years, and he has not come to business yet." REGINALD YOUNG (who has been. very attentive 3u ring the evening)—" I wonder, Miss Mabel, if you ivould consider me impertinent should I ask you the old question" Miss Mabel (greatly agitated)—"Oh, Reginald.l This is so sudden—l—r—yes, I will Itisten to you, Reginald." Reginald Young—" Well Alien, have you read 'Robert Eismere ? ' "—Atlanta ,Journal. - _ .

A meeting was held to endeavour to persuade him and others to join the dissentients. Argument. failed, and at length Dr. Candlish said, "Let RS pray for our brother," 'whereon our svvitherer came out with " Corae, come Candlish, none of your hrtmbug," and left the TOOTR, IYRIO'. catechising by the Scottish clergy was nary the minister of Coldingham, in Berwick- as.ced a simply country wife who resided at the farm of Coldingham Law, which was always styled "the Law" for brevity's sake, "How many tables, Janet, are there in the law 2" "Indeed, sir, I canna jist be certain," was the simply reply ; "but I think there's ane in the fore room, ane in the back room, an' another upstain." A SUBURBAN widower married a second time, I and his choice was a wealthy lady about 50 years of age. When the bride and bridegroom returned home from the wedding, the husband, introducing his wife to his children, said, "My dear children, kiss this lady. She is the new mamma I promised to bring you." After taking a steady look at the "new mamma," little Charlie said, "Pa, you have been cheated I tribe isn't new at all 1" THE minister of a parish in Scotland was called In some time ago to effect a reconciliation between a fisherman of a certain village and his wife. After using all the arguments in his power to convince the offending husband that it was unmanly in him, to say the least of it, to strike Polly with his fist, the minister concluded—" David, you know that the wife is the weaker vessel, and you should have pity on her." "Well, then," said David, sulky, "if she's the weaker vessel she should car,y the less INVENTOR—"I have just perfected a machine to—" His wife—" Yes, that's it. Why don't you invent a machine to help me with my work, instead of inventing something to do the work for the men so that they can loaf about and drink beer?" Inventor—" That's just what I have done. I've invented a contrivance that will save two-thirds of your time," Wife—" Is that so? Your are a dear darling of a husband after all! What is it you have invented for me " Inventor—" A talking' machine." TALKING recently to t mother and her daughter, as swell foolishly observed—" Really, Miss your mother looks younger than you do 1" Then, realising from the young lady's flashing glance that he had terribly missed the compliment he sought to give the mother, he hastened to add—" Because, you see, the older a woman is the more time she has had for mastering the art of looking young." And now mother and daughter "cut him dead." "John, your hair is coming out at a terrible rate.* Husband—" I know it is, old woman. I mast do something for it at once." Wife—" I wish you would, John, for my sake. You know how people will talk."

THE IDEAL OF GRATITUDE.

When a person has been saved from the agonies of a terrible and untimely death, or, indeed, when he has avoided intense suffering of any kind, it is only natural that he should be grateful, and desire that others should be benefited by his fortunate experience. Such has been the inspiration of every testimonial regarding Warner's "SAFE" Cure which has been given to the public. The following is published with the hope that the afflicted may be benefited :—Mr. P. Brown, 45, Primrose Road, Marsh Lane, near Liverpool, writes: "Last May I found myself out of health, with a miserable swelling of the feet and legs, which I could not get rid of. I kept getting worse rapidly, and finally had to take to my bed and have medical attendance. The doctor said, after a care- ful examination, that I had Bright's disease, and told my wife I could not recover, and would not live beyond a month. All this time I had a most horrible and distress- ing sickness, could keep nothing on my stomach, and would have such violent fits of retching and straining that I had to be held. I had heard good accounts of Warner's SAFE' Cure, and, as the doctor could do noth- ing for me, my wife sent for a bottle and began to give it to me in small but frequent doses. At first I had it in water, and it soon quieted my stomach. I began to improve after a few days of its use, and when the doctor came he said he never saw such an improvement, and was completely surprised. Not desiring to deceive him, I told him.what I was taking. Most extraordinary!' he exclaimed. I continued the remedy, and after three months of serious illness, during which I was given up to die, I again resumed my business. I have praised War- ner's 6AFE Cure tar and near."

div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."
I hear that Captain O'Shea will probably become a candidate for a seat in Parliament in the Unionist interest.
Prince Victor Napoleon recently passed ten days with the ex-Empress Eugenie at Farnborough. It used to be understood that the Napoleans were not on speaking terms with each other.
Henry Irving is a Mason. Pinero is a Mason, Augustus Harris, W. Terris, Corney Grain, and many other theatrical people are Masons. They are spoken of in the " Masonic Review" as Brothers."

The Quakers of Ohio are "reforming " in a manner their progenitors would not have desired. In that American State a proposal is under consideration that each Friends' meeting should have a settled pastor.

The bill for the amendment of the Factory Acts which the Government intend to bring in will, it is understood, raise the limit of age at which children may be employed in factories to 12, and the age up to which they may be employed in underground mines to 14. The employment of women within a month after childbirth will be prohibited.

It is an interesting fact that, in spite of all the troubles of the political situation—and perhaps we might say because of them—the fight at Bassetiaw is being most vigorously maintained. The Liberals have a first-rate candidate in Mr. John Mellor, and he is getting a very large following. Mr. Schnad- horst is taking a particular interest in the contest, and is doing his best for the Liberal champion.

We have some reason to believe that, in spite of Lord Wenlock's appointment, the Government pro- pose to retain Lord Connemara in his post as Gover- nor of Madras for some time longer, be being desirous of entertaining the Cezarewitch as the representative of the Queen. That such a scandal should be seriously contemplated may seem inc:e- ditable. But the best remedy in these cases is timely publicity.

A well-posted London correspondent- the Pnnce of Wales is bent ,0n..-rellSilning the late- ness of society's dinn i kir hour, which for the future s to be fixed for eight. At present it is practically nine; which is simply prepo,terous, preventing playgoin,g, early rest, and other pleasant and healthful enjoyment. But if 11.R.H. is to dine at eight, how about the Royal eggs and bacon with the so-called five o'clock tea, of which rumour speaketh ?

The ten-year-old Queen of Holland is by no means unlike her aunt, the Duchess of Albany. She has been brought up in the simplest possible manner, under the direct personal superintendence of her mother, Queen Emma, assisted by a professor and an English governess, Miss Winter. She has always been accustomed to play with the children of her late father's humbler neighbours, and was never so happy as when entertaining her little friends sand facon at the Loo.

A good story was current in the lobby on Monday evening concerning the long-drawn-out Parnell meeting. Mr. Labouchere is credited with having gone up to Mr. Akers-Douglas, the Government whip, and asked for the " loan" of Mr. W. H. Smith for a few minutes. " What for ?" was Mr. Akers- Douglas's natural inquiry. "Well," replied the hon. member forNorthatnpton, "we want him to go up to the Irish meeting and move the closure."

The member to whom Mr. Parnell referred as having given him a stab in the back, and as the "leader-killer," was Mr. John Barry. Mr. Parnell's own professions of loyalty to Mr. Butt are ridicul- ously untrue. Those who can recall the period in which the two men were in the house together will recollect that Mr. Parnell constantly Routed Mr. Butt's leadership. He often treated his recommen- -1 dations with contempt and / recollect that more than once Mr. Butt was deeply affected by the con- duct of his headstrong follower. No man was ever less submissive to a leader than Mr. Parnell, and no one as leader has ever exacted more abject submis- sion.

Mr. Robert Barr, better known as "Luke Rharp; tile well-known American humorist, who edits the London. edition of the "Detroit Free Press," anti contributes a story to the Christmas number of that paper, has been engaged for many years in turning out "funny stories." - He is one of the most brilli- ant and most successful of American humorists,and, in fpite of all temptations, is still a Britisher. Mr. Barr was born in Glasgow, but, finding that there was little demand for fun in his native city. left for Canada at the age of four, taking a young Glasgow accent and his old parents with him.

The University College. Aberystwith,, has reason to be proud, for it was ahead last week of all the colleges in the kingdom in the number of students who took their B.A. in London. This is all the more creditable, as the difficulties of the college are great. One has lately arisen in the tendency of the Denominational Colleges in Wales to gravi- tate to Cardiff and to Bangor. This, however, will turn in the end to the advantage of the University College, provided that it firmly resists any attempt to make its scholarshins close, and that it keeps its standard as high as possible.

The Queen is very gratified at the unprecedented success which her stock sent from Windsor gained at the Birmingham Cattle Show,for of seven entries, six won first prize in their class, while the seventh second. Moreover, her Majesty won the three special prizes offered for the best Hereford., the best Shorthorn, and the best Devon ; while, to crown' all, the Devon took the prize given by Lord Aylesford, the president ot the Birmingham and Midland Counties Association, for the best animal in the show bred by the exhibitor ; and the Shorthorn then won the Elkington Challenge Cup of 100 guineas for the best animal in the cattle class. This cup becomes the Queen's property, as she has now won it two years consecutively.

I LIFE OF MR. PETER RYLANDS. I THE ELECTION IN ST. JOHN'S WARD.

By L. GORDON RYLANDS, B.A. (Continued.) This result, so unexpected, since the close of the poll, by both parties, was due to the fact, in the midst of confusion caused by a great pressure of voters, some seventy or eighty of Mr. Greenall's
supporters gave in t'heir voting .cards, not to the
i;ut to one of the che—ck-clerics acting in Mr. Greens,ll's behalf. The men then left the booth
under the impression that they had voted. The check-clerk entered the votes in the check-book, but
in the hurry and confusion prevailing at the time omitted to see that they were properly entered in the poll-book. The result was that Mr. Rylands had , .
a majority of recorded votes. The leading Conserva- tives demanded that under these circumstances the election should be declared null and void. The

Mayor, however, considered that he had only to do with the official poll-book, and held it to be his duty to return Mr. Rylands as member, maintaining, also, that Mr. Rylands cmild not legally refuse his elec- tion, even if he wished.

The Tories were very angry at this decision. They accused the Ma 3 or of partiality, and called upon him to resign. But the Mayor, Mr. Nield, acted ex- tremely well all through the difficult circumstances in which he was placed—he disregarded abuse, and did his duty without flinching. When Mr. Greenall's friends found they could pro- . .. .

duce no impression upon the Mayor, they decide 'd to lodge a petition against Mr. Rylands' return. This they did, and Mr. Baron Martin was appointed to try the case. The question was really a very simple

one, and after hearing all the evidence tlie judge gave his decision to the effect that if there had been any omission to record in the poll-book votes which were "legally tendered," it would be his duty to order those votes to be added to the list, and to give the candidate in whose behalf they were tendered the benefit of them ; that the legal tender of a vote consisted in the voter giving his name to the poll- clerk, and telling that functionary for whom he polled; that in the case considered it had been proved that the votes in dispute had not been ten- dered to the poll-clerk at all; that the giving in of the cards to somebody who happened to be sitting at the table was not the legal tender of votes; that, consequently, the votes in question were not lost, for they were never recorded; that they were not recorded because they were not tendered ; and that, in fine, to say the election ought, on that account, to be declared void, was an absurd and ridiculous proposition." This election was certainly:a remarkable one. Possibly no case precisely similar has ever been recorded ; never- theless a similiar result might conceivably Occur under our present system of ballet voting, for, suppose the majority of the elected candidate were very small, say 5, and suppose there were 30 spoiled votes ; now it is quite possible that 20 of these spoiled votes might be intended for the beaten candidate and 10 for the victorious one, in which case the successful candidate would represent a minority of voters. But no one would dream of de- manding that an election should be declared void because a number of votes were " spoiled," that it not " legally tendered," or that an attempt should be made to discover which candidate each spoiled vote was intended for, in order that the candidates might be credited with them. Therefore the taunt, which was on one or two occasions subsequently directed against Mr. Rylands by the Tory Press, and once by a Tory member of Parliament, that he was the member for the minority of Warrington, was utterly without point. Mr. Rylaads himself had no scruples about taking the seat he had just won, because he telt convinced that about 200 of his supporters had been tampered with, and prevented from voting, and that, if the election had been fairly fought, he would have had a considerable majority. He, therefore,. con- sidered himself no less morally than legally the member for Warrington. I do not intend to dwell at length upon the variou!jt

cidents of Mr. Ryland'j_Lar..lla..___ _ Q.O.fiterri the perusal of the correspond- ence to which this sketch is an introduction, and of Mr. Rylands' speeches, which are published in a separate volume. 1 shall merely refer briefly to some of the more important questions with which he was concerned. Mr. Itylands was extremely well fitted, both by natural ability, and by long training, to take at once a leading position in the House of Commons. The ex- perience which he had been gaining for so many years in the miniature parliament of Warrington Town Coun- cil, had made him a ready debater and practised in deal- ing with public questions; while his natural busineSs ability, and his close acquaintancewith business matters, not only caused him to look at all public questions from a thoroughly common-sense point of view, but especially Qualified him to form an opinion upon financial and economical affairs. He, therefore, saw with great dis- gust the extravagence which characterised (as it still does) the great spending departments of the State, more especially the naval and military departments, and the Diplomatic Service ; and, as he never hesitated to con- demn wasteful expenditure, irrespective of the party responsible for it, he soon obtained a reputation for sturdy independence. He also identified himself with, the cause of Social Progress, particularly with regard to the liquor traffic, on which subject he not only moved' several resolutions, but was one of the promoters of a= Rill in the sessions of 1870 and 1871 to prohibit the sal&

of liquors on Sunday. He also became a vice-president of the License Amendment League, the chairman of th:4 Warrington branch of the National Education League, a member of the committee of the London Chamber a . . .

Commerce, a member of the Cobden Club, a member of the committee of the Land Reform Association, and a vice-president of the National Union for the Suppression of Intemperance; and in many other ways showed his sympathy with the cause of social and economical se- form. His activity during the years 1889,74 was very great, and the subjects to which he devoted himself very numerous ; indeed, so intensely had he applied himself to his public duties that his health was much impaired ..but he had the satisfaction of feeling that he had woo for himself a considerable reputation and a leading potion among the advanced section of Radicals. No doubt he expected that the .Warrington electors— especially now they had protection of the ballot—would reward his labours by returning him again to Parliament by a large majority.; but, as everyone knows, a wave of ' Tory re-action swept over England in 1874, and, in com- pany with a large number of Linerals, Mr Rylends was overthrown by it. His total poll on this occasion was 2,201. while Mr. Greenall's was 2,381, the latter being, therefore, elected by a majtaity, of 180. Mr. Rylands thereupon accepted an invitation to con- test South-East Lancashire—a forlorn hope. The two Liberal candidates spared no pains, but were defeated by a considerable majority. Although Mr. Rylands was disappointed at being thus excluded from the new Parliament, it was really by no means a disadvantage to him, for he stood sadly in need of rest, and was enabled, in 1878, to return with renewed vigour to the House of Commons as member for Burnley, a far more satisfactory constituency to him than War- rington had been. • The Conservatives beine, now in office, Mr. Rylands felt more free than he had previously been to criticise wasteful expenditure, and to denounce jobs and abuses of all kinds. He also turned his attention to foreign questions, and often spoke, both in Parliament and in the country, in opposition to the foreign policy of Lord Beaconsfield, whom he distrusted profoundly, and whose methods he considered most dangerous. All through this Parliament again this energy was remarkable, and the range of subjects of which he made himself master very wide; but his lthours undoubtedly told still further upon his health. In, 1880 Mr. Rylands was again elected member for Burnley by an increased majority. He looked with pleasureable anticipation to the future, for the Liberal party was again in power,and Mr. Gladstone's Midlothian speeches gave promise of much prosperity to the coun- try from prudent adminstration and wise and progressive legislation. But the event was very different, and as time went on Mr. Rylands began to find Parliamentary life distasteful, and began gradually to lose confidence in the leader whom he had hitherto enthusiastically admired. He entirely disapproved of much of the foreign policy of the Government, and was particularly disgusted with their discreditable mismanagement of Egyptian affairs ; but the measure of his annoyance was I filled up by their vacillation in regard to Ireland. He welcomed the Land Bill, and he believed that, if it had a fair chance, it would go very far towards pacifying Irish I discontent; and he could scarcely find words to express his contempt for the weakness of the Government in not making up their minds .bodly to try the effect Of a gen- erous policy of conciliation in Ireland. In private he denounced the Coercion Bill in strong terms, affirming his belief that the whole effect of the Land Bill would be neutralised by it, and of Mr. W. E. Forster he never could speak without irritation. He attempted in the House of Commons to give practical effect to the opinions he entertained on this subject, but was immediately so inundated with remonstrances from his constituents in Burnley, Who implored him not to embarrass Mr. Glad- stone, that he sank his independence, and, by his votes, supported a measure which he detested. This was a very bitter experience for a man of such strong convictions and such independeace of character as Mr. Rylands. He writhed under the compulsion to which he yielded, and the whole volume of his pent-up wrath was directed against Mr. Gladstone. It was Mr. Gladstone who, as head of the Government, was responsible for his mis- taken policy, and it was the remarkable influence of Mr. Gladstone upon men that led his constituents to insist upon their member's loyalty to his leader. It was Mr. Gladstone, therefore, whom Mr. Rylands made respon- sible for the humiliation he felt in voting one way while his convictions pointed in another. (To be continued.)

The election of a councillor to succeed Mr. John Platt—who has been raised to the aldermancy—in the representation of St. John's Ward, Warrington, took place on Monday. The contest was fought politically, the Liberal candidate being Mr. Felix Loughlin, jeweller, Buttermarket-st., and the Con- servative candidate Mr. James Hill, builder, 23, Birehalt-st. The polling booth was the club-room, in John-st., and there were three polling stations, naniely, polling station No. 1, for voters on the bur- gess roll, division,l, from 3,058 to 3,517; polling station No. 2, for voters, division 1, from 3,518 to 4,016; and polling station No. 3, for voters. division 1, from 4,017 to 4,272; and division 3, from 7,612 to 7,715, all inclusive. In all there are 1,319 voters in the ward, and at the last election in November, ' 430 .of these voted for Mr. G. Blackhurst, the suc- cessful Liberal candidate, and 392 for Mr. Hill, who was also the Conservative candidate at that time. On this occasion both parties to a great extent concentrated their forces on the Ward, and, as a consequence, the poll was much heavier than in November, although the contest was con- ducted in a very quiet manner. The returning officer of the Ward is Alderman Sutton and the officials at the polling booth were as follows :—Not 1 polling station : Presiding officer.. Mr. W. H. Wood- cock; poll clerk, Mr. W. Smith; personation agents; Messrs. Kean and Lyons ; polling station No. 2; pre- siding officer, Mr. J. J. Smith; poll clerk, Mr. Geo. Riley, and personation agents Messrs. Walter Bate and J. J. Ashworth ; polling station N. 3: presiding officer, Mr. Edward Gibbon; poll clerk, Mr. E. Whittle, and personation agents Messrs. Thomas Jackson and John Mullins. Amongst the election literature put out was the cor- respondence between Mr. Loughlin and Aldbrman Platt which we published last week, and Mr. lieughlin also found it necessary to issue copies of the following tele- gram from Alderman Platt: "Llandudno, Nov. 29. Clayton Liberal Club. Hill's statement that I wished him every success is not correct." The Conservatives scattered broadcast on placard and handbill "seven reasons" for voting for the " popular " candidate, Mr. Hill. The Conservatives believed that Mr. Loughlin's prospects of return were ruined from the moment the Parnell difficulty commenced, and the result proved that they were right. The ballot boxes were removed to the Council Cham- ber at the Town Hall shortly after eight o'clock.„ where the counting was proceeded with in the presence of the Returning Officer (Alderman Sutton), the Town, Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), the Conservative candidate (Mr. Hill), the Liberal agent (Mr. John Clayton), the Conser- vative agent (Mr. John Hanipson) Mr. Kiernan, and others. It was found that the niimber of votes recorded was 1,081, which included four spoilt voting papers, three of which had been put into the ballot box in exactly the same condition as received. In the other case the burgess had voted for both of the candidates. The , Returning Officer declareathe result of the poll aa fol- lows :-- , (C) Loughlin (L),

After tha declaration of the poll there was a consider- able gathering at the Liberal Club. Amongst those pee- sent were Councillen.F.: A. Rbberts (who presided. Councill'or-W:Pierpoint;.E Meriting. and H. Roberta,. Mr. F. Loughlin, the candidate-011r. Jahn Walker, Mr. WI. Robertsf Councillor F. A. Llaranrs said, that although he was not with -them on the- ISt November they congratulated themselves on their vietories,andthey must not be down- hearted zrovr because,. on the gross results, they still showed an improvedpesition in the Town Council ion what they had twelve months ago. (Hear, hear.) Ile was veiy sorry they could not congratulate Mr. Loughlimon having won the seat in St. Jcan'S Ward. They knew he had worked very hard. and he (Mr. Roberts) know a great many who hnd worked very hard for him. They had been defeated, and defeated by a large majority,,but that would only make them raore determined to win.: on the nest opportunity. Ile was satisfied thas it had been their little diffieultlea of the meent and net the senee--of the wand that had been shovvn that day. (Hear,, hear.), Some of them had been agitated in their,. mind's- lately, and a good many of their friends bad, ho- was afraid, thought they would. wait to see how, things went in the polfitical horizon before they went to-poll any more. He believed, however, that baize the next election came round, they would be able to carry Mr. Laughlin with a good majCritV• tie, ,as an Englishman' was particularir sorry that Mr. Loughha, an Irishman, had not won the cause that day. (Hear, hear.) In times like that they all had great sympathy with their Grand Old Man in his trouble, and he was glad to say that Mrs. Loughlin had the-same symnathy with them. (Applause.) He'thought the,- must thank Mr. Loughlin and Mr. Loughlin— ' (apPlause)—and Irishmen generally, for the active fight they had waged that day. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Loughlin hnd entered the fight as the Liberal candidaht and he was the defeated Liberal candidate—he meant in the broad sense andmot because Mr. Loughlin wasan Irish- man and the representative of Irishmen in Warrington Be moved that they tender Mr. Loughlin' their best thanks for the active contest he had engaged , ('Applause.)

CouncillOrnumanta expressed his extreme regret that Mr. Loughlin was at the bottom of the poll.. It was not the fault of the leaders of the party, but of some of the weak-kneed Liberals, (Hear, hear.) It was not the fault of the leaders; for they had put Mr.-Loughlin for. ward as a Liberal, and a true Liberal, andi be (Councillor Fleming), was-more sorry-at the result than:if he hadelost the election himself. There had been a../ot of religious bigotry and intolerance brought into that-contest ; he had himself found it in the canvass. (Hear, hear.) They all lived together in this country—Engtishmen, Seotch- men,.and Irishmen—as one nation, and -why these things should have been imported into the contest heaven only knew. (Hear, hear.) Mr. LOUGHLIN, who was loudly cheered, sal& he felt I very much for the result of that appeal to the e4ectors,,l not so mach on his own account, but because ha had the: feeling that perhaps another man wculd have veon—(no, no) —bat on reflection he was almost inclined to think that they should have had a hard struggle that day in- any candidate. There had been many thins against him these last few weeks, and he had beea no sootier started than there was this last great catastrophe in their party. (Hear, hear.) He could assure them he VTGA at one with Englishmen on that poinhe was entirely with Mr. Gladstone and the Li,beral party. (Applause.) He had never wavered in his, opiruca that after the verdict 'inMr. ParirelPs case was Scordad, Mr. Parnell conld no longer be the leader of the Irish cause. (Hear,. bear.)a Although Mr. Parnell's c,olleagues, out of sympathy with, him when he was under a cloud. had, re-elecaed, him, leader they had no mandate to do so from the Irish, people. (Hear, hear.) He believed that matter had had an influence on that election, ad he was, told it would have. He did not suppose that any other candidate in Warrington had had to contend with what he had had to contend- with in that electan. (Hear, hear.) Every imaginable thing had been brought in. When it was not nationahty it was creed, and when it was not creed it -was the leadership. His epponentshad rung the charges upon these in every imaginable way; and a gentleman, who was not a. voter in the ward, had said to him "Mr. Loughlin, after ad that has been said against You if you are hr to-night it is nothingshort of a miracle:" He honestly believed that, after what had been said about him,. it would have been a miracle if he had carried the seat. (Hear, hear.) fie should have been content had the election, beea fought on its merits, as to whether Mr. Hill was or was not a better man than him- self. Of course, the otlites ,side had proved themselves right, and it wasallownitrat bigotry was still a • power amongst them. (ffear,eliear.) He was sorry it was so, and he had t.) appeal to his countrymen to be easy and resigned. A better time would come, for- surely the clouds would lift some time and they should have a little sunshine.' (Hear, hear, and applause.) ,He quite admitted that circumstances had been all. against them, but he should not like to close his remarks ---wlthout sag how much he thanked tha workers. On that occasion he could say that the leaders of the Liberal party were with him heart and koul, and he could say that day after day one or' the other I had been with him dirvassing. (Hear, hear,)- They

had that day had more workers than they could find work for, and few candidates could say that. (Hear, hear.) It was just possible that under the circum- stances, no Liberal could have carried that seat, though probably another Might have been defeated by a reduced majority, and he regretted the defeat not so much on his own account ; he was somewhat east Mills mind when he was assured by those likely to knew the state of the Liberal party that he was not the one who had caused the loss of the seat. (Hear, hear. and applause.) Councillor 11. ROBERTS said he thought their candidate had borne his defeat like a man, and in fact there had been in that election such an appeal to the basest passions that men were unfortunately endowed with, that not even the angel Gabriel himself, bad he been the Liberal candidate, could possibly have won. (Hear, hear'and , langhter4 He was quite convinced in his own mind that there was nceblame whatever attaching to the'can- didate. He did not want to begin throwing stones in their own ranks, ask was not good policy, but he lieved that the very' men who had not been faithful to the party would be the first to regret the result next morning. (Hear, hear.) It was no use blinking the fact they had to thank for their defeat one manand that was Charles Stewart Partied (" No, no" and " Yes, yes.,")' That was his•opinkm, and he was net one of those who,. having an opinion,,was afraid to utter it. said agaira as an old electioneerer, that they had to thank one man and one man alone for the defeat and that man was Mr. Charles Stewart Parnell. (Hear, hear.) They had been , defeated that day, but the present condition of ; things would not last long. Because they had lost that election they were not going to ; throw up the sponge. (Applause.) He believed that 'after the present darkness a light would &me that 'would last for many years, and he believed there would be greater cohesidn. in their ranks than ever before. He had heard it over' and over again in that election that any stiek was good enough to beat the Liberal candidate with. It was. the keeping of an Irish- man and a Catholic out of the Town Council—that was thesum and substance of the whole position. Alderman Harrison said the other night that if they voted for Mr. Loughlin they voted for an alien in race, an alien in religion, and an alien in he did not know how rsany things besides. Yet they graciously permitted these aliensto live amongst them and to be taxed for their benefit, but when the time came for a 'privilege to he extended to them it was refused. That' was the spirit that had always dominated the Tory party and always would till it changed it nature. (Hear, hear.) He could assure Mr. Loughlin that he did not think the ' majority would have been less against 'any other man. (Applause.) Cheers' were then given for Mr. and 'Mrs. Loughlin and • the meeting terminated.

A STARTLING Itu In order to understand tlie circumstances under which Ruric was brought before the Emperor,it will be necessaay to go back a few hours, The autocrat had occasion to send for the surgeon, Ropani, who had attended at the duel, and as he was some time in answering thesnmmons he was questioned, when hedid come, conctrning his tardiness. His answer was, that he had! been attending the' Count Da- monoft

" bud What ails the Count r asked the Emperor. " He was well yesterday." " Yes—but he met with an accident to-day." " Look ye, Kopani,''' the young ruler cried, who saw in au instant that something unusual. had hap' penod, "'think not to conceal anything from, me. What is it now?"

"Sire, meant not to. hide anything fromtyou. The Count has been engaged in a duel.' " !was be challenged,?" " No, sire—he wai the challenger." " So, so. And who was the'other party F "An hunable" gun-maker, sire, named. 'Ulric Linvel." " Nevel—Nevel—" soliloanized Peter. "The•name
is familiar."

" His father was a captain in The last war with the Turks. He arose from the ranks under.F6odor, and was one of the bravest of the brave." 't Captain Nevel—Ah, yes. I remember now% . He and Valdai were the tvvo who first moanted the ramparts at Izium. So the old idispatches read.' " Yes, sire. Poor Nevel was shot a month •after- wards while leading his brave company against a whole squadromf Ttirkiah infantry, while•Vildai came home and got a colonen-commission."

"And afterwards received a•title," added %ter. "Yes, sire." "And this gon.maker is thistaptain's so'? , Yes, sire." "And methinks Valdai left a child." "'He did,[sire---a daughter, whb is novv•with Olga —she is his ward." "Yes, yes. And the COunt fought a • duelwith young Navel, Mid got beaten,eh [ Before the surgeon could answer, a page entered the chamber and announced that the Duke of Tula wished to see hisrimperial master. • The Emperor direded that- he should be ad- [ gated ; and ere Icing afterwards the proud Duke entered the apartment. He was a tall, stout man, with light hair and blue eyes, and not far from five- [and-forty years of age. • the bearing was haughty, [ though he was forced to 11 tallow of respeet now that be was before his master.. "Sire," spoke the Duke, afser the usualtanta- Ikons had passed, "-I have come to demandtinstice at thy hands. My young friend, the Count Conrad Dernonoffi has beennsost brutalLy murdered.'r "Ha! Say ye oes Olga?' "Yes, sire." ' "But[how was inn

"Thus it was ire: : On the - day before yester- d'ay, I sent the COunt with anessage to one Ratio Novel, who,ia a gun maker in Sloboda.. lie went as I wished,. and while there, the guns maker, who is a huge fellow, provoked a quarrel, and knocked the noblomart down. Of.course the‘Count wae offended, and .as the ruillan threatened to re- peat the offence, end as he furthermore grossly in- sulted a noble lady whom tho-Count held most dear, he could hardly help challenging him, Thltotellow --,,ted the challenge, and haa succeeded„ by the inflicting noon him
"Because, sire, he descended from his station and etruck me. He threw away the shield, which should protect the nobleman, and ,struck me with- out provocation." "And then you knocked him down?"
" I did, sir." -------- - "And perhaps you would have done the same to
"Sire, answered the youth quickly, "when Damonoll tried by threats to make me sign his paper I told bite there was but one man on earth at _
Wliose order I would do t-ht-t- thing. The man who hae the rigid to command shall never have occasion to strike me."
Tkere was something in this reply, and more in the tone and bearing of him who spoke it, that made the duke tremble. lie saw plainly that the Emperor's eyes sparkled with admiration as thoy
rested avow the gun-maker. • "'Slut now about this duet: resumed the Emperor "flow dared yowtake advantage of the count in the 1 conflict r
"Advantage, ave.?" repeated the youth, in surprise.. " Aye. Did,he not„Stephen limn? " " did, sire," replied the man thus addressed. . . . .

"And which of 'the two do, you call the best swordeman?'" Peter-asked. "Why, sire—the count is, or was, vastly his superior." " Andl what, say voul.sir lieutenant ? " Alarm trembled, for this wax- addressed to him. He knew; that the duke-was anxious to crush his friend, and he feared, to draw the wrath of that powerful nobleman down upon, his head. But a happy thought came-to his aid- .. Sirel: he said," kwould rather you, would judge of that for yourseifr "Me judge ? And how. am I to, do that?" , "Let Runic Nevelskill be tried here before you. 'lf I mistake not you, have some good swords- men near your palace. There is Demetrius the Greek.'"
"What—my Mistevai-Arms??' "
"Why—he is the beet•swordeman in- my empire, I think our young adventurer would fare badly in his hands."
"Never mind, sire Ivou could jpdge." " Whyr 'said Peter-with ag smile, "Demetrius handles-the count as Ilwould a. mere _

Sireir Spoke Rutio,-.modestly,. but not frankly, "It wassurely no diegrace to he. overcome by your tutor!'" "Ands will you take it, turn, with, him at the swords P. " Yesoire--if so it please yous"" "By my soul," eriedethe Emperor- leaping UP " wellies's° some diversions out,ot this-trial. 1% hat he, there ! Light upthe chamber. Let every lamp be lighted, for we want sight now. Send Demo- - trius here—and tell him to Meng hieround-edged swords V T Both the duke andUrzenstood aghast at this new turn, but”they dared not interfere,, for they saw that their imperial master was all excitement now to see a trial of skill at that science which, above all others, he tried to .make his officers learn. But then they ,had •one- hope: :Demetrius might over- - come the gun-maker so easily that Peter should not see, his real power. Demetrius soon. came, and under his arm he car- ried the swords. They were- of the common size,. . but with round edges and points on purpose for • The master-at-arms was-a powerfully . built !man, and possessed:. a. splendid form. He was a Gree:it,lsy birth,, and. was now retained by the • Emperor as a teacher of the sword exercise. " Demetrius," said Peter,."-I have sent for you to • entertain us withsashow, oh your skill. Here is a ::man about whose- power there is some dispute. Mind you—it is ellin,kindness.--Ruric Nevel, take • your:weapon!! The youth stepped forward and extended his left.; hand for the sword,, and the-right hand he extended. for the other to grasp, it was taken warmly, for the Greek saw in-an-instant that he had a noble • mars to deal with.. And those two men were not .1- much unlike in form. Demetrius was an atom the • taller, but Ruria.showed the most muscle. The night ,hed come-on, but the great lamps were-fl alLlig,hted, and therooat was as bright as day. "-Sir," said Ruric„addreesing the Greek, " this, is- • none of my.seeking, though I will confess that tor. 7 a long while I'have longed to cross a playful sword with you. I play. well." " I like you,' the Greek returned, bluntly and: kindly; "and if you, beat me I will not like you less.- keen afford to be-beat once, seeing that thus far, ,I ; have never been-since first I offered to fence." " Come, come, cried Peter, who VAS impatient for,- the entertainment, "let's see the • opening. New, itand gentlemen." Like twins stood those swordsmen as their - weapons crossed with a clear, sharp clang... The off Greek led o carefully, and Ruric as carefully warded every stroke. Then the former assumed -a- , guard, and Rurie led off in turn. Ere long the swords clashed with sharper ring, and soon sparke- d fire flew out from.the clanging steel. Louder and louder grew the clang, and quicker and quicker - grew the stroke& The thrusts were made with -skill-, and force,lgut as yet neither had been touched. The nraperor was in ecstasy. He clappsal his hands and shouted bravado with all his might.. , andby Ituric's eye grew more intense in its sparkling-nre. His opponent saw it, but he -could not telLwhat it meant. The youth was about tO risk the most daring feat of all he knew.. Steadily burned/hiseye, and his lips were set like steel. it length he saw that the Greek was playing, for so. thrust;.and he lowered his point. Demetriue. saw the ohance,.and drawing his arm quickly, back, he Made the thrust with all his power. He was, sure . now he-had won, for there was no earthly, way in which his-point could be struck either down or up. • But see!! With a gliding motion-7-a motion, almost impere,eptiNe--Rurie raises his sword and the other slides -along upon its side, and the other point,, in- stead of touching his breast, is caught in the cross- guard of his haft. Then, ,quick as lightning, and with alibis might, Rurio,bends his elbow, down- ward with the whole weight of his massive shoulder, and throws his wrist upward. On that -instant the Greek sees and feels what meant that strange line of - the eye.,. He feels his point caught, but, before he can close his grasp more firmly the haftiis.wrenched from,hishand—it strikes the vaulted ceiling with a dull clang—And, descending, is caughttfairly- on the ;hilt by Ruric Nevel Foramoment all as death inthat chamber. Rurieeis the first to break the silence., He-advances - to the. Greek, and, as lie hands back both the. swords, he-says: "-Demetrius, remember your promise. I know yon are a brave man, for I can see it-in year forgiv- ing glance. You wiltuot like me los fer,•tkie By heaven, no !" the noble Greek cries, drop- ping both the s-words, and extending both hands, which the gun-maker grasped. "-I, honor you—l Love you." Peter Alexiowitzi the impetuous- Emperor—then in the zeal and fire of youth—leaped from-his stand-- ing-place, and,caught Rune by. the hand. "By Saint Michael !" he cried, earnestly andd loudly, " yonstand clear of all blame, for full well do I know that,rhad you so osired,, you could harne slain Conrad Earoonoff at your, first thrust." "Sire," returned the youth,,now speaking tremu.-• lously, " twice did I disarm the count, and yet spare, him. Atid,whesa, in my ragej, broke his weaponin twain tosbring him to his senses, he seized a second. sword." "Sir Duke,' spoke the Emperor, turning towards' Olga, who stood trembling with rage and martin: - cation, "you see you must have labored under a mistake. Tett. can retire now —not a, words sir 'Mae quiverino lip and a trembling step, the e• duke left the apartment; and after him, went Stephen rrzen. `4l‘Tow,.lturic Nevel. if you leave Moscow without nag, consent. you do so, at your peril. Ilwould not We sight of you. You are at liberty." In an, hour more Rurie was upon his mother's 'bosom.. He told her all that had happened—all but the last words of the Emperor. He did not, tell her 'of those, for he knew not whether they boded him goed or evil.
(Ta be continued.)

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was'held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Frazeomb) presided, and there •were also present Aldermen Harrison, Wright, Holmes, Platt, Davies, Burgess, Sutton; Councillors W. Pierpoint, R. T. Fairclough, Cannel], Garner, Shaw Green, Beaman, .Ashton, Hill, Dixon, Taylor, Hepherd, Muir, Voisey, Hutchinson, Browne, F. W. Monks, Flood, Fleming, Jenkins, H. Roberts, Bolton, Heaton; Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Longdin (borough sur- veyor), Chorley (borough treasurer). • THE DEATH or ME. SLIMES, MOW.

Alderman Divms asked for the indulgence of the Council while he made a sad communication to tbsm. He wished to refer to the death of Mr. Samuel Rigby, which occurred that morning. He was sere it would be a matter of grief and pain to all the members of the Council—(hear, hear)—to hear of the death of so res- pected a man, a man who some ten or more years ago identified himself with Warringtonin every movement of progress, in every movement in the promotion of its trade,andamanwhowarmlydid his hest in the in- terests of Warrington, and in connection with all objects of charity. (Hear, hear.) He did not know that he had, felt the death of a man so much as the felt the death of Mr. Rigby, and he thought he was at that moment -speaking the feeling of the members of that• Council. • (Hear, hear.) There must be many who ha 4 a warm memory of Mr. Rigby, and he was sure that his name would not ,readily die in the minds of those who knew him. He begged to move "That the members of this•Counoil desire to ex- press, and record their acknowledgment of the valuable services rendered to the town, trade, and charities of Warrington, by the late Mr. Samuel Rigby, who died this morning, and that their deep sympathy and con- dolence be conveyed to his bereaved widow on her sad loss." (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS said he begged to second the reso- lution. He did not know any circumstances in the; whole of his municipal career thathad given'hion-such-al shock as the announcement then made by Alderman, Davies with reference to the death of Mr. Rigby. That. was the first intimation he had received of Mr. Rigby2s demise. Alderman HARMON .oh, indeed. Continuing, Alderman BURGESS said he • could Msure them it was a painful thing to him, for he hadsknoivn . . . . . . .

Mr. Rigby's standing in Warrington; what fte.isad done' for Warrington, and what he was always • desirous of doing, not only for Warrington, but tvhereverhe might be situated, to alleviate distress and to aid and assist his- fellow men under all circumstances. (Applause.) They would not soon see another Mr. Rigbyin Warrington. He - could have wished that, he had not•ha.dthat, painful duty, to discharge; but letit be known to the bereaved widow, • and to the members of his family, that in Warrington, and in that Council Chamber especially, Mr. Rigby had : left behind him, audit would not-soon pass away, from ' the members of that Council—a knowledge that he faithfully did his duty. , (Applause.) Councillor Dixon said from the time.he became AC- . • quainted with Mr. Rigby up to the present, their rela- tions had never been strained. Wherever he had met • with him he had always been the same Mr. Rigby -as he • was when he first knew him. He was a gentleman, the like of whom, during.a life time, thepeould net find many. Mr. Rigby was alwaymready whenever he (Mr. • Dixon) appealed to him, to give information and help - and personally he greatly felt his loss. , (Hear, hear.) • Councillor lictraiNson said he was slue theynuistall feel that they had lost a very generous and good-hearted friend and personally he had•known Mr.. Rigby, for agood litany years—ever since he corns .to Warriegton, and he , (Mr. Hutchinson) alway,s found him to bc.a thorough, gentleman, and he was sure it ..was a_greet loss to the r. town to loose such a valuable friend. . _
The vote of condolence was then carried unanimously. ELECTION ,OF 4COUNGIL.LOES.
The MAYOIL reported that Mr. F. Monks had been , elected a councillor for Whiteeross .Ward; and Mr. :James I Hill councillor for St.-John's Ward.
RIELLONXISON•OF Lk. IBISLEY.

The PLlvoit stated that he had.reeeived the following t. latter from Mr. Tinsley Thelwall,lflth Nov. 1890. - To the Town Cdezk of the Borough .of sWare.ngton. hereby resign my position as Camellior of the Latchford Ward of the Borough, audi hereby tender the amount of the fine of such resignation.—Yours truly, Wilautt '.7.nruzy." The Mayor continued that Mr. Tinsley had i=paid his fine, and the Council had theano option, but to declare the office vacant. •

THE NUISANCE IN SAKEENTST. , The MAYOR moved the adoption of the .minutes. of . the v.Watch Committee. „Alderman HARRISON seconded. Ccancillor FLEMING said be wished tosaf.a.few words before those minutes were passed. ks the.y .were.aware, i.he was appointed a member of the Watch Committee, :the .Council thinking because he resided near.Sankey-st., -that,he would be able to abate the nuisanceiathat street. ilt,had been his duty for a few Sundays back to,petam- bulate that street, but he had not fouad any nuisance. Be found that there were people in the street, but how were they to get rid of them.? they had as much .right ; there, as the members of the Council had. Wear., hear.) So, far he had seen, order existed in the.atteet., „(Ap- plause.) Alden:nen BURGESS said he also had been an observer, not tar the purpose of finding fault, but to see what took , -place. Ile thought there had been some improvement; 4 but haves not by any means the paradise that Councillor ;Fleming represented it. The complaint had been that the street was taken possession of by a number. of people . who appeared to have no avocation whatever. The :footpathwas an impassable path for ordinary travellers and he ,(Alderman Burgess) wanted to know whether they were going to be shouldered off by three, four, or five, perhaPs,young girls or young boys,walkizig abreast, laughiugotcrea,ming and enjoying themselves. Alderman HARRISON: Let them enjoy themselves. Aldermau BURGESS continuing, said not at all, at least Mot at his, expense. He thought they had a perfect right to use the street, and he expected that the Watch C.:situnittee mould see that Sankey-st.. was not a bare ,garden thatdt had been for months and months, and that the police would keep order, and move people on and not ;let them.ta.ke up the street in the way they did. Counciller Mum said he had seen a lot of silly girls and youngloys talking and laughing; but they could not get the police to take these people into custody. Alderman BURGESS: No one wants that. Councillor WIEL : Well, how would you rectify it. Alderman floutiEss : By keeping them in order. Councillor DixoN stated that only last Sunday night; shortly past eight o'clock he, in company with a friend, came up Bold-st. and along Sankey-st. to see what they had to contend with. flethought there were about ten or twelve persons standing on the parapet this completely blocking the way, and he and his friend were obliged to take the centre of the road. They went a little further, and found a crowd of five or six, and at another place there WU also a crowd; and opposite the Park-gates there were from 25 t 0.30 persons standing. He suggested some years ago that the Mayor should give instructions that people be not allowed to stand on the parapet. He went to various towns, and if they took Birmingham-- (laughter)—they would not find the same nuisance existed. The MAYON said he thought Mr. Fleming deserved, the thanks of the Watch 'Committee for parading the street on Sunday nights. ble(the Mayor)had gone through Sankey-street on a Sunday evenings a great many times; but he had never seen what Alderman Burgess complained of, a lot of young boys and girls, who were, perhaps, making the street a sort of meeting place. He thought they would always have boys and girls amongst them who would laugh and joke, (Hear, hear.) The difficulty to his mind was, how were they to move them ? The greatest nuisance he had seen in the streets of Warring- ton were at the coroner of Bank-st., and Dolman's-lane, were men congregated and spat about the place. This pointed him to the fact that they should widen out the neighbourhood of Sankey-st., and make a proper promen- ade for the young people to walk on. (Laughter.) The minutes were then adopted. ALDERMAN DAVIES ON THE FINANCES.

Them. mutes of the Finance Committee were moved by Alderman Holmes and seconded by Councillor Shaw- Green, but before they were put by the Mayor, Alderman DAVIES said he thought it was very necessary, now that the new Council was framed, that they should make some estimate as to the finan- cial position of the borough. The reason he thought this was necessary was because various candidates and others on the platforms had made promises of what they were going to do, if they were elected to the Council, and it was therefore, essential that some one should suggest the dssirability of not over-running the constable. He wished to say that he was not making any reflection upon what any member of the Council was going to propose ; but he would ask them to consider what they had done financially, likewise let them think of what was going to be done. (Hear, hear.) They had just obtained an Act of Parliament which had dbst £3,500, avd the borough treasurer assured him that it would cost that sum at the least. That, in the first place was a matter to be borne in mind. In addition to the purchase of the gas works, they had bought the water works at a 30 years' purchase. He had nothing to say against the purchase; all lra wished them to do was to bear their financial position in mind, ad be prepared to bear an additional rate of id. or 2d. in the pound for the next few years in respect of that achievement. One gentleman had promised the public that they were to have three baths ; he had nothing to say against that being accomplished, but he would say let them be sure that they cou!d raise the money for the improvement without harassing the ratepayer's pocket. Another gentleman had suggested that they should make the library free. Again, he did not object to that ; he rather sympathised with the proposal, but, at the same time, it could not be done without means and funds. Another individual said he was going to move the depots altogether. (Laughter). With reference to the extension of the borough, they must bear in mind one thing—and he was open to cor- rection if it was not so—that they would have to enlarge their appliances at Longford, because they would have

to remove much more excreta than before. Since the extension of the borough they had undertaken a very serious responsibility in taking over a great number, or great lengths of roads, that had hitherto been under the direction of the County Council oir the Rural Sanitary Authority. In addition to that they would have to pro- vide new lamps over the new district ; •ind that was very urgent. They also would require more police, but some might answer to this that they had an additional rating of the property in the out-lying district. Like- wise they must bear in mind, and admit, that the rating ' of an outside district was not at all commensurate with the mohey that would be expended in other respects, for it ives a very small rating power. Again, they mightshortly, perhaps,be asked to raise a stun of £5,0D0 for the purpose of developing a technical school, .and this was not a thing to be neglected. He had next to sneak in reference to the question on which Councillor Roberts intended to touch npon that evening—the ad- visibility of declaring ,expenses incurred in the paving of (private streets to be private improvement expenses. He (Mr. Roberts) asked for the consideration of the Tax- ing and Sewering Committee to be given to the matter; but he ((Alderman Davies) might tell the Council that it was not a(question concerning that Committee, but was a matter entirely for the consideration of the Finance Committee. Councillor ROBERTS : I explained that that was my own idea. I was advised by the Town Clerk to make the .recommendation to the Paving and Sewering Committee. The Towx CLERK: And I gave that advice 'because the Committee had consideredit.

Alderman DAVIES said the Paving and Sewering Com- mittee were only street makers, and had no power to con- ,sider any financial question whatever. It was purely a ifinancialquestion, and he would invite the Council to allow Mr. Roberts to discuss the question on'that'Com- mitte's minutes. and he might say, from his own point of 'view, and in the interests of the Council, toat whatever • the deliberationsof• the Committee might be, the Council had to conform and abide by them. In his opinion the making of a street was as much as the making of the , houses or appurtenances. They must not be under the ;impression that the builders of houses were suffering more to day than what thebuildersof houses did in days gone by. On the contrary, more convenieneesand 'ties were given themat the present time, than there were ' .15 years ago ; .and he would submit that the -cost of making streetsto day, as compared with 15 years ago, was 30 per cent. less. (Hear, hear.) Allthese were what ,he called immediate financial interests for that Corpora- lion to consider. He believed that very night a. very important meeting was being held in Manchester, to con- sider whether local authurities and urban authorities should not be required toput in. force the Rivers Pollution Act, in nrder to prevent the pollution of rivers. lit was -also desirable that it should be knownthat many of the ;main sewers in'Warrington -should be relaid. In con- , elusion he would say to the members of the Council who had been newly elected, as well as to the older members that they must not be too rash in spendingmoney. (Ap- i,plause) Alderman BURGESS said there were one or two points e that had been raised by Alderman Davies that seemed to _place them in-such a gloomy position in the future that he thought not-one of them would dare to, do anything that they ;.knew they ought to do. lest they should level the town in -.some/ serious difficulty. the Borongh ;Treasurer was -a great authority with him on anything 'which had reference' to the finances of that Council. He would like to know, for he had not anticipated it, if -"E3.500 would berequired to be paid by that Corporation for the bill for the extension of the borough, and for the amquisition of the waterworks. The ISIXYOR said the Town Clerk had told him that until the accounts had been taxed i no one knew how' much they. would have to pay. The amount of M,500 might be nghtor it might be wrong. •Adlerman DUB/Gass: I- should like to know what the oosts.are untaxed. rIheI3OIIOIIGH.TREASURE/i : There are some eut-stand- iingaccounts.

viEdermanßutmess said he thought the matter ought not to have been brought before them that night ,unless they knew what they had to pay. Someone •certainly had furnished Alderman • Davies with the information he had given them, and that somebodY, he should think, was present, and would be able to ix- . plain the matter; but, if there was no explanation, he would leave it to the future. lie thad listened with a degree of ,satisfaction to the statements of Alderman , Davies, and it was ezceedingly desirable that the mem- bers of that Council should know their financial position, for thereNva.e the poembility of their getting so far in ,advanoe that they might find it a matter of serious diffi- culty • hereafter. Be, however, ,hardly thought they were going to get over the line. The extension of the ' , borough., and the acquisition of the .waterworks would mot entail &sixpence additional expense with regard toi. the works at Longforet; and it would be remembered that he told the Commissioner during. is visit to War-z .rington. that the money being asked for then would' suffice' forko,ooo more inhabitants. .Soar as the sewers' were concerned, whether they liked t or not, and, Whether the, people of the town liked it ,er not, the time .ws& not fardistant when-the Paving and &wenn Corn-: mittee, or some COmmittee of that Corporation. would hare to undertake, at a very big cost, the reconstruc- , time of the syStern of sewers generally in the borough; butso far as the river's pollution was concerned, he did not think that need give them much concern. It was a tidal river, and there was no power, so far as he knew, that,could.rearth thakCorporation for turning the sewage into that river, that he believed to be the law. He 'hoped, in conclusion, that the Corporation was not going 1 to get into any ficancial difficulty as Alderman Davies appeared to be afraid of, and be .felt they would never evantanappraiserso long as Afderman Davies was in the I Council to guide them in the expenditure of their money. I(Applause.) , Alderman SurroN said they could all satisfy them- selves that whenever those various questions came be- fore the Council, they would be considered in a proper way, and with due regard to their financialposition at the same time.. (Hear, hear.) It was always a very pleasing thing to know that they were progressing in- stead of retrogressing. As often as those matters were brought forward, so long as they were for the good of the town, and in the interests of the ratepayers, without going too deeply into details, he was sure they would all be willing to carry such measures. e, however,thought that the advice given by Alderman Davies would be fairly looked to at the tune when it was necessary to do so.

Alderman HOLMES stated that there was good reason for saying that £3,500 would be required for the exten- sion of the Borough Act. He was of opinion,however,that the cost would not be beyond that amount. It was al- ready provided for, as two calls had been made upon the overeeers of the poor of £1,500 each, and the first call had been paid. (Hear, hear,) The minutes were then adopted. ,

This Committee recommended that Alderman Platt be chairman, arliP Alderman Sutton vice-chairman, for the ensuing year. Also, that the following members of the Committee be appointed the Lighting Sub-Committee The Chairman, Alderman Wright (Convener), Councillors Blackhurst, Bolton, and Muir ; and that the following members be appointed a Visiting Committee to visit the sites of proposed buildings or alterations to buildings when required :—The Chairman, the Deputy-Chairman (Convener). Alderman Wright, Councillors Bolton, Muir, and Henry Roberts. Mr. Councillor PIERPOINT, having intimated his desire to retire from this Committee, it was resolved that his resignation be accepted, and Mr. Councillor Dixon ap- pointed in his stead. That the plans of the following buildings be approved :—Two houses in Arpley-st., for Mr. D. Ain ; five houses in Chorley-st., for John Platt, Esq. ; additions to Hawthorne Inn, Orford-lane, for Messrs. Whitley, and Co.; shippon and premises in Orford-lane, for Mr. Lashford. Alderman PLATT moved the confirmation of the minutes. He said the work of lighting the extended 1 borough was proceeding. In Alderman Davies' statement there had been one point left out and that was that Bridge-st. and Horsemarket-st. could not be kept in their present position for a very great length of time. When the borough was enlarged he thought the question of widening those streets would be forced upon them. He quite agreed with Alderman Davies that they would have to be very careful how they spent their money, because there would be occasions when they would have to spend. Alderman WRIGHT seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor DIXON objected to the appointment of Ald- erman Sutton as deputy chairman as ho thought that position ought to be given to someone who was not al- ready on the General Purposes Committee. He moved that Councillor Blackhurst be appointed instead. Councillor BLACHIMRST, however, pointed out that he' too was already on the General Purposes Committee. Alderman SUTTON and Alderman PLATT both contended that a deputy-chairman ought to be appointed on the grounds of his claims and fitness, and not merely with a view of putting him on the General Purposes Committee. The minutes were adopted. THE SANITARY COMMITTEE.

This Committee had passed the following resolu- tions :—That Mr. Alderman Wright and Councillors Hepherd and Henry Roberts be appointed a sub-com- mittee to superintend the horses, vans, stables, and pro- vender, and all matters pertaining thereto, and to report to this Committee (Mr. Alderman Wright to be the Con- vener) ; that the Chairman, Deputy-Chairman, and Councillors Flood and Henry Roberts be appointed sub- committee to visit the Infectious Diseases Hospital, and to report to this Committee; that the Chairman, Deputy-Chairman, Mr. Alderman Wright, and Councillors Beaman, Voisey, and Walker be appointed a sub-committee to visit the Longford and Intercepting DepOts,and to report to this Committee; that the sum of £2B 10s. be paid to Mr.. Thomas Ford, of Latchford, as compensation for the loss of one cow and three calves, slaughtered by order of this Committee in consequence of an outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia on his premises; that Mr. John Fair be appointed salesman for the sale of concentrated manure manufactured at Long- ford, subject to the terms and conditions of an agreement to be prepared by the Town Clerk; that Mr. Joseph Bibby be also appointed salesman for the sale of concen- rated manure, on the like terms and conditions.

The Paving and 'Sewerage Committee recommended that the following apportionments of the cost of forming and paving Helsbp-st. and Stephen-st. be approved, and that the Town Clerk be instructed to recover the amount due from each owner—HeZsby-st J. Rigby, 30, Robson- , st., £43 Is. ltd..; Ellen Anderson, 23, Helsby-sti., £24 12s: sd. ; J. Marsh, 3, Rolleston-St., £3B Is. 30.; J. Bottomley,so, Church-st., £3B 14s. 9d.; T. Littlewood, Winwick-st., £42 145. lid.; Thomas Whittle, Butter- market-street, £3B 12s. id.; Land and Property Invest- ment Company, per Messrs. T. and J. L. Tunstall and Co., £l2O Bs. ; Colonel Blackburne, per J. White, £l5 Bs. 3d. ; total, £357 14s. 7d.—Stephen-st The Land and Property Investment Company, per Messrs. T. and J. L. 'Tunstall k Co., £llO 7s. id; the Corporation of Warrington, £lB 14s. 10d; total £129 Is- 11d. Als the Borough Surveyor having submitted plans, specifica- tions, and estimates, for the forming and paving of Leonard-st. and Laira-st., resolved that the Town Clerk serve the necessarynotices upon the owners for the form- ing and paving Of the above streets and that the Corporation execute the necessary works in the event of the owners being in default; that a sewer be constructed in the new street off Marsh House-lane near the Barracks; that the offer of Mr. Robert Heaton to purchase a plot of land and five cottages in Bostock-st., belonging to the Corporationbeaccepted. Alderman DAVIES, lU moving the confirmation of the minutes' explained that the plot of land and five cottages in'Bostodk-et., which .Mr. Robert Heaton had offered to purchase, was property acquired by the Corporation in default of payment for street making by aMR named Longshaw. It necessitated their fighting an action for the recovery of that money at Liverpool, and the result was that they gained the day, but like many other men who had fought a good battle and won they had very bloody noses. (Loud 'laughter.) He did not intend that as a reflection upon any individual. As they knew a Corporation could kick, but could not be kicked. He added that the total apportionment of Helsby-st. was 'E357 15s. id. Alderman Warour seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor BLAUICIIIIRST said that several of the tenants kad drawn his attention to the condition of Dial-street, and he expressed a hope that the Committee would have it-repaired. Councillor FLEMING said that Fennel-street was in a worse state than Dial-street ' • it was in a disgraceful con- dition. Hamilton-street, Birchall-street, and other streets in that neighbourhood also needed attention. The Baron observed that Hamilton-street and Bir- chall-street were at the present time under notice for paving. Councillor BROWNE a§ked whether any other offers for the land sold to Councillor Heaton were received by the Committee, and if the land had been publicly offered for sale ? In addition to the streets which had been named, there was Bank-street—a most important street—(hear, hear, and laughter)—which was paved with large cobbles that were a nuisancq not only to pedestrians but to car- riages and carts. The County Court judge had often to stop in the middle of a vase because of the noise made by passing vehicles. Alderman Sorrow: Ton should get a better place for the Court. Councillor JENKINS complained of the bad state of the macadam roads in the borough, and that the work of re- pairing, when done, was carried out in the summer in- stead ,of the winter. Councillor DIXON said the had received a complaint from Mrs. Willis respecting the condition of Crossley-st., and Back Crossley-st. The MAYOR: Is there any other gentleman who has any special property to look after ? (Laughter.) Councillor FAIRCLOUGH said he would like to complain about the street leading to Mersey Mills. (Laughter.) It was 7ft. under water last week. _ .

The MAYOR : Is that not Councillor Fairclough's pri- vate occupation road? (Laughter.) Alderman DAVIES said that tenders for paving Birehall- st. had been accented, and the work would be proceeded with at once. Dial-st. should be attended to forthwith. Fennel-st. had been a constant complaint of Councillor Fleming, and the Committee could not, he was afraid, make it into a new street. Bank-st. was not such an im- portant street after all. (Laughter.) It was true the County Court, ably represented by Alderman Harrison --(laughter)—was there, but many people in the town 'would be quite satisfied if the Judge stayed away alto- gether. (Renewed laughter) The bad state of many of the streets was largely due to the recent heavy rainfall. With respect to Longshawls property, it was offered for sale by auction, but was not got rid of. The Committee had made and received offers, and Councillor Heaton's Offer was the best they had,received. The minutes were confirmed.

f on before the magistrates; and fines inflicted in all cases. The average attendance of the public elementary schools during the month of October was 8,219, corres- ponding period last year, 7,921. Increase 298. Councillor FLEMIN6 moved the confirmation of the minutes and referred to the action of the Committee with regard to the examinations. Councillor SHAW GREEN, in seconding, said that ow- ing to the system of examinations by sample' a great many hardships had arisen. Some of the school masters very wisely put on their schedules the names of all the boys eligible to sit and consequently the bulk of them got a certificate. Some of the schoolmasters did not take this precaution and many of the boys who would otherwise have passed are compelled to attend school tlll the next examination. Councillor Ptarr hoped the Committee would press their application because he found it was a serious griev- ance with a great many people. In answer to Alderman Burgess, Councillor FLEMING said a boy could leave school at 13 if he had passed a cer- tain examination. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH asked if it were not the fault of the schoolmasters where these cases had not been brought forward. Councillor Snew GREEN said that it was so. It was assumed that every parent knew the regulations, but there was not one in a hundred who really did so. The schoolmistress did, however, and those who did not put the scholars on were to blame. The minutes were then adopted. THE XIISECTIS COMMITTEE.—A FREE LIBRARY AND A TECHNICAL SCHOOL.

N. Houghton; fourphotographs taken in thei Museum, from Mr. P. Dalton; parcel of local pamphlets and broadsides, &c., and collection of Australian ferns, from Mr. R. Davies; drawing of archceoptery, in frame, fromldr. F. W. Monks; " The River Mersey," by W. Spiriks, from the Author; Baedeker's Handbooks, hcc. (8 vols.), from Mr. R. Pierpoint ; "David's Reserve and Rescue;" a sermon before the House of Commons, by C. Herles, Pastor of Winwick, 1645, from Alderman Davies. It was resolved that the thanks of the Committee be sent to T. W. D. Houghton for the case which he had caused to be provided for the picture, "A Mountain Farm," by Clarence Whaite. Uouncillor H. ROBERTS, in moving the confirmation of the :minutes, said that Alderman Davies in his finan- cial statement might also have mentioned that the mem- bers.of the Museum Committee were bound in honour to make the library free as soon as the extra rate came into operation. They had given pledges to that effect both as member of the committee and of the Council, and he should like it to 'go forth to the public that there would be no doubt about that being done. Councillor PIERPOINT seconded the confirmation of the minutes. _ _ .

Councillor Straw GREEN said they had heard of a pro- posal to raise some £5,000 for technical schools but even if that were done it would not cost that Corporation more than id. in the 2. They were not empowered to spend more than id. in the 2. The minutes were then confirmed. ,CEMETERY COMMITTEE.
