illuminating power of the gas during the past three weeks had been equal to 18•8;eandles at both works. Alderman Homaas moved, and Councillor FAIRCLOLIGII Seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor Dfxow drew attention to the poor quality of the gas during the past two or three weeks. He said that since he had baen elected he had scarcely gone down the street once without being stopped by someone , —frem the clergyman downwards—with a complaint about the gas. He did not know that he had ever seen Bold.st. Chapel so dark as it was on Sunday evening; the worshippers could not see each other. The Mayon said he thought it would be a very good plan for the Gas Committee to appoint a sort of commis- sion to go thoroughly into the matter. (Hear, hear.) On Monday evening, in the Mayor's parlour, it was al- most impossible to see. At the present moment in that Council Chamber there was something desperately wrong with the gas. They were told that it was on account of the pipes not being sufficiently large to carry the gas from the street to the Town Hall. When hewent to live at Wilderspool he could scarcely see by the light of the gas supplied to his house. On sending a complaint to the Gas Works, he was told that the meter was too small. He obtained a larger meter, and now had as good gas as it was possible for anybody to have. There must be something radically wrong with the Bold-st. Chapel. A commission ought certainly to be appointed to discover why certain buildings obtained good, and others bad, light. Aldermen DAVIES remarked that it was intended to make use of the photometer at the Town Hall, so that the quality of the gas might be tested there as well as at the gas works. On some occasions the gas was good enough, but on others it was not good enough. If, as was stated, the poor light was due to the smallness of the bore of the pipes, it would not fluctuate as it did at present. (Hear, hear.) Having referred to some criticism of the Gas Committee, he went on to say that ' the purchase of the gas works had not cost the Corpora- tion one farthing; the whole sum had been paid out of the profits of the concern. After alluding to the profits made, and the reductions in the price of gas, he said that altogether the borough had benefited to the extent of a capital sum of £113,474 18s. by the purchase of the gas works. Councillor VOISEY said that Alderman Davies's statement would have been all the more interesting if he had explained why the expenditure last year was so much greater than the year before, and what the Committee intended doing with the surplus of £2,000 which, in addition to all the allowances and payments mentioned, their accounts showed. (Hear, hear.) - •

, Councillor HENRY ROBERTS remarked that the com- plaints of the bad quality of the gas had been unceasing for a considerable period, and it was quite time that the Committee made strenuous efforts to supply a better quality of gas than had been the case for many years past. With respect to the figures which had been given by Alderman Davies, he would like to ask, touching the saving of £24,000 to the consumers, whether the ledgers showed saving to the gas consumers as between the amount of their accounts to-day and the amount of their accounts a year or two ago ? (Hear, hear, and" No.") He regretted to say that, so far, he had not met with any , case where men had come forward and said that as the result of the reduction in the price of gas their accounts had been less than when the price was higher. To explain that curious anomaly was more than he could do. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Then, as to the £l,OOO contributed towards the reduction of the rates, the Council were unaware whether that sum was taken out of the profits of one year or out of the accumulated pro- fits, and unless the Committee would guarantee the con- tinance of that payment year by year, it was somewhat absurd to capitalize it. (Hear, hear.) Councillor HEATON said that on Monday evening at Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' offices the gas was so bad that each of the clerks had to work by the light of a candle. On being tested the light was found to be short of 16 candles. Councillor BOLTON suggested that the maximum and minimum illuminating power be given each month. It was a farce to give only the average. On the previous night he saw four candles which gave almost as much light as six gas-jets. Councillor Fairclough, who was a member of the Gas Committee, had stated that his gas bill was less than it used to be. His (Councillor Bolton's) was doubled. (Laughter.) Councillor Fainctouoil explained that he was referring to the gas bill for the National Schools, of which he was treasurer. Many more meetings had been held there since the Rev. F. W. Willis came to Warrington, and yet the gas bill waslower than had been the case for several years. (Laughter.) Alderman &mons said it might be the nature of the worship was of a superior character to that of Bold-st. Chapel, but the lighting of the Parish Church on Sunday evening was everything that could be desired. His own experience ot gas bills had been a curious one. Some years ago his gas bill persistently travelled upwards, so that in seven or eight years the quantity of gas consumed, or supposed to be consumed, at his house trebled itself, beat after reaching a certain summit it began to travel downwards, until at the present time the bills were the lowost he had ever had. (Laughter.) Councillor HEATON : That is the result of going to the gas office. (Hear, hear.) Councilior Mims gave notice that on some future occasion he would move that the price of gas be reduced. _ .

Councillor Dixow : Hear, hear; I will second that. (Laughter.l Alderman HOLMES said he did not admit that the quantity of gas was at all defective. There might be, and probably was, a lessening in the amount of pressure which was put on, but that was a very different thing from poor quality of the gas. With reference to

the complaint from Bewsey Forge, he must admit that on Sunday and Monday nights there wei e failures at the gas works, concerning which he had that morning received an explanation from the gas manager. Mr. Haddock had suggested that if the Gas Committee were dissatisfied he was quite willing to have an expert examine the works and see whether there was any failure which might be remedied. The service pipes all over the town were being enlarged for the express purpose of pro- viding the inhabitants with a good supply of gas. Re- specting the financial part of the matter, he believed that the accounts showed the condition of affairs thoroughly. The Committee wished to keep nothing back. .

The MAYOR said he did not think anybody doubted the capacity of Mr. Haddock, but when Councillor Dixon stated that Bold-street Chapel was in darkness whilst, according to Alderman Burgess, the Parish Church was beautifully lighted, there must be something wrong. It would, therefore, be well if the Committee got two or three people to visit the works and the churches and chapels, and see what was the cause of all the grumbling. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then confirmed. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommended thal the following mem- bers be appointed the Parliamentary Sub-Committee The Mayor; Aldermen Burgess, Davies, Chandley, Holmes, Sutton, Wright, Platt; Cciuncillors Pierpoint, and Fairclough. Also, that the following members be appointed the Open Spaces Sub-Cominittee :—The Mayor, Aldermen Holmes (Convener), Davies, Wright, Platt ; Councillor Henry Roberts. The minutes were confirmed. THE PAVING OF THE STREETS.—PRIVATE IMPROVEMENTS. Councillor H. ROBERTS moved :—" That the Paving and Sewerage Committee be requested to consider, and to report at an early date to this Council, upon the advis- ability of dliarin,g expenses incurred in the paving of private streets to be private improvement expenses, and of making arrangements for allowing to the owners of property concerned therein a period of years for the pay- ment of their apportionments of the cost of such pri- vate improvements." He held, he said, that it was one of the primary duties of the Corporation was, so far as they possibly could, to secure that the dwellings in which the ratepayers had to live should be as healthy in their surroundings as possible. That being the ease, no one could have gone through the different wards—as many members of the Council had during the past few weeks—without becoming painfully impressed with the fact that very large areas were in a condition which was not only insanitary and dangerous to health, but positively disgraceful to the Corporation and the town at large. (Hear, hear.) He believed that up to the present time the Committee had done their best to deal with the large and increasing difficulty which faced them. But, there was in the first place, no systematic arrangement as to the order in which streets should be paved. It was most unfair that a man who built property say in IBBB,should be compelled to make the street with- in 12 months or two years of that time, when, on the other hand, there were houses which had been erected for eight, ten, or twelve years, the streets for which were not yet made, or even in contemplation. (Hear, hear.) His proposal would not put upon the Corporation any further responsibility than italready had. Alderman Davies hinted at the possibility of the Corporation run- ning a risk in lending money to builders or owners of property ; but he (Councillor Roberts) had it on the authority of the Toww Clerk that there was no necessity to mortgage the property. Any debt to the Corporation would be regarded as a first charge on the property, and would have priority over a mortgage. It had been said that the cost of making' the street was really a part of the cost of building the house and he was quite pre- pared to admit that argument, but they had already in thousands of cases assisted the purchase of property. He referred to the work of building societies which had assisted tbousands of property owners. The principle had been conceded and had been proved to work well and satisfactorily all round. He knew that the officials of the Corporation were as lenient as they could be in carry- ing out the present system, but in spite of that it led to hardship. He knew of one case in particular in which the cost of street making for five cottages was something over £lO5, and the owner not being able to meet the claim at the time had to realise at a loss of £9O. (Hear, hear.) Since he gave notice of that motion he had been approached by many people asking him to press the matter as strongly as he could. His resolution only asked that the Committee [should go thoroughly into the matter and report in detail either for or against the proposal. His object was not to benefit particularly the builders, but to assist small owners of property. It was to the advantage of the Council to encourage build- ing in the borough, and that would be one way of doing it. (Hear, hear.) Councillor FLOOD seconded the motion which was agreed to.

div.head: ATTEMPTED MURDER AT WIGAN.
div.p: ATTEMPTED MURDER AT WIGAN.

Joseph Turner, 19, was brought before the Wigan magistra' es on Monday morning charged with attempt- ing to murder William Campbell, hairdresser, Wigan. The Chief Constable prosecuted, and Mr. Tarbuck ap- peared for the prisoner. Turner was formerly employed by Mr. Campbell, but was discharged for misconduct. On the 24th ultimo he intimated to two persons that be was going to shoot his old employer, and about half-past six entered Mr. Campbell's shop and fired two shots at him. One bullet struck the latter in the right side, causing a superficial wound under the armpit, and the other hit him at the junction of the head and neck, but fortunately struck the skull at the hardest part, and de- flected outwards. Ih reply to Mr. Tarbuck, witness said prisoner was strange and excitable in his manner when seen before the assault. Campbell was sufficiently re- covered to be present and give evidence. The prisoner was committed for trial at the Liverpool Assizes, and the presiding magistrate at the close said the Legislature had imposed restrictions on the sale of poisons, and there ought certainly to be more stringent regulations as to the sale of revolvers and cartridges.

div.head: TRIAL AND SENTENCE OF MRS. FEARCY.
div.p: TRIAL AND SENTENCE OF MRS. FEARCY.

At the Old Bailey, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Den man, the trial was commenced of Mary Eleanor Pearcy alias Wheeler, on the charge of murdering Mrs. Hogg and her infant at Kentish Town, Mr. Forrest Fulton opened the case for the prosecution, and said it was important for the jury to know that intimacy had taken place between Frank Hogg and his wife before he mar- ried her. At that time Hogg was also 0.11 the closest terms of intimacy with the prisoner. Mr. Fulton read letters which had passed revealing the nature of these relations, and John Charles Pearcy deposed that, in co n- sequence of the prisoner's intimacy with Hogg, he ceased live with her. Frank Samuel Hogg. deceased's hus- band, said he first had immoral relations with the prisoner about a month after he was married. His wife had no knowledge of it. William Henry Holmes, a boy twelve years of age, living in Prince of Wales-road, stated that on the day of the murder the prisoner gave him a note to take to Mrs. Hogg at 141, Prince of Wales- road. Re-examined, he said he identified the prisoner by her face and hat. He was alone when he picked her out. A number of other witnesses having been exam- ined, the Court adjourned: On Tuesday evidence was given by the local police of the discovery of Mrs. Hogg's body at Hampstead. The detectives spoke to finding the body of the child, and to the condition of Mrs. Pearcy's house. The female searcher at Kentish Town Police. Station repeated her statement as to the version Mrs. Pearcy gave her of the origin of a dispute preceding the murder.—Dr. Bond said he believed that the scalp was first injured and that the throat was then cut. Much force was necessary. He found scratches on the prisoner's hands, as if from glass. The blood-stained carving knife found could not have inflicted the wound on the neck .—Dr. Jeeper gave similar testimony, and said that the smaller knife shown him might have done it. This concluded the case for the prosecution.—Hr. Hutton having intimated that he did not propose to call witnesses for the defence, the counsel ' tor the Crown summed up the case, and then Mr. Hutton addressed the jury on behalf of the prisoner He sub- mitted that the case was entirely one of circumstantial evidence, and evidence of a kind which it would be most dangerous to accept as conclusive, especially as the jury would have noticed that the prisoner, had she been guilty, might easily have escaped, or tried to do so.—The further hearing of the case was adjourned until Wednes- day morning. On Wednesday, Mr. Justice Denman summed up adversely to the prisoner, and was very severe in his denunciation of the conduct of Hogg, the murdered woman's husbond. The jury found the prisoner guilty ; and in reply to the usual question why the death sen- tence should not be passed she declared her innocence. She bore the sentence without any outward expression of emotion.

PROMPT ATTENTION TO ORDERS.

The Dark Days Mr, PARIMLL is to, be deposed • of from the leadersl4- of the Irish Rome Rule. 7garty ; and. lie is. to be deposed unatk ,-circumstauees which render- it impossible - art he can evar, again be, thoroughly trusted. Tan.day.s ago he stood in the position of one who • exited some syrapathy.-bacause,, although he had sinned, he was being ,mada suar- ha more than an ordinary degree;- and iihe had: then voluntarily retired from a position whieh ha could no longer • retain with credit to- hirnself-orhis party, it would no-Vhave been without tha -hope that a day would came ..when he would, again be recognised as a leader of the Natio:nalistai. But to-day he is not airobject of sympathy he is a creature to be despised; for, finding that he could no longer be • captain of the ship in .whieh he, was sailing, he has • done-the best he could smite*, it. He isutterly • demoralised, and in hisclosperation it would seem that there is nothinghe.will not do to irjuro the • men- and the cause- wilh were supposed . to be so dear, to hita. Petristiam !: There is no such sentiment in, him;- for- his person;' claims are set before evcuything else. Ale began ~ with wrecking; the- honour of a woman and the liappiness of, al family-;: and he follows it up by .46nlonstrating: beyond the possibility of a doubt that he cannot be- relied, upon to keer 'faith either r With man or woman.. His malignant manifesto waS--c )ntended to, cast refrection upon theatharacter of.f Mr; GLADSTONE: as the man who objeetted to stand, Side by side with an adulterer im leading and,o directing the forces of Home Rule. It was devils• work, and it has brought devirs pay. The boomerang has returned, full cirAe, and staick:c down theman who hurled it in the air. Mr. GiAn- 'STONE has replied, and Mr. PARN_OLL stands cOll- - 'clemnecl, Nobody doubts the we:d of the lea,e'r of? the Liberal party, while the wiek's achievement of the leader of the Irish, party is that.— 'he has ceased to be regardech as a statesman,. and his word is no longer talx.o. To-day he is • not merely the discrowned—he is the 'dishonoured king. He may be a force for :evil: in politics, but he is no lonea a power for good,. for he appears to have said with Milton's "Satan" :—" EViI be thou my good'.".' In one week he has i tried conclusions with threaleading Engliab statee. !men, and sought to show that they were untrue to Ireland; but in the result there is no ,perktly proved except that of Csannas STEWART ,PARWII,L. As for Mr. GLADSTONE, he comes out a the, en- counter with hands thatl were always c'aian,, -wear- ing as ever "the wEte flower Of a blameless life," the revered of his countrymen, the beloved; eaf his party, the Grand Old; Man. But what, it is being asked, is to be the. end of this disturbance and, disruption? The-abandon- . meat of the Hornaß'.ule cause ? Not =Or -a.inoment. It has been said a, hundred times that the agita- tion would go On even. if Mr. GLAWTONR, were to. be removed; and it must go on,. if need be, with Mr. PA%NilliD, as the draff, on the wheel. The immorality, or political suicide), of an indivi- dual is as nothing to the interests: of a nation. The Liberals have taken up the, carte of Home Rule because they believe that it will be just to Ireland and beneficial to England.. Ireland blocks the way, and there is no going round, no escaping the block, however much the. difficulties of its removal may be increased. We may for a time lose elections, as elections lisate already been lost in Manchester and Warrington; but the loss of elections cannot, in the long run, be so disastrous —to put it on the lowest ground—as the loss or desertion of principle. We must think, too, of the gallant body of Irishmen, who are giving their feelings a wrench in sacrificing Mr. PARNELL with the object of saving the cause. Ties of the strong- est kind bind many of them to their late leader; but the ties which bind them to their country and their countrymen are stronger, and they are to be honoured and upheld in the part they are taking. They have behind them, and will continue to have behind them, the majority of the people of Ireland, while Mr. PARNELL will be left to pursue a guerilla warfare with mal-contents and in s.chief-rnalrers. It would be a fitting punishment that he who has even stood aloof from the Plan of Campaign should be driven to rely for support upon the conspirators: and ne'er-do-weels who have been the bane of every movement for the redemption of Ireland. Bat, come what may, "forward "is the word. Home Rule for Ireland is but the precursor of Home Rule all round. Each of the four nations of which the United Kingdom is composed is suffering because of the incapacity of the Imperial Parlia- ment to deal efficiently with domestic as well as Imperial affairs. There are a score of reforms of which the country stands sorely in need, but they cannot be secured in the deadlock which it is the delight of a Tory Government to maintain. The land of promise is before us; there must be no turning back because Mr. PARNELt can no longer be trusted as the leader of the Irish people.
The Eight IT is pretty generally conceded Hours by advanced politicians, that a Question, good case has been made out for Parliamentary restriction of the work of miners
, I

div.head: TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: TOUCH AND GO."

to eight hours a day; but when it comes to a question of applying similiar restriction to every trade it is seen that it might conflict in so many ways with the interests of both employers and employed, that there are comparatively few who make a stand in its favour. Still, the subject is under discussion, and it ought to remain under discussion until what may be gained on one side, and what may be lost on the other, are fully un- derstood. A generation has passed by since Jonic STUART MILL said :—" Hitherto it is questionable if all the mechanical inventions yet made have lightened the day's toil of any human being. They have enabled a greater proportion to live the same life of drugery anti imprisonment, and an increased number of manufacturers and others to make fortunes. They have increased the com- forts of the middle classes; but they have not yet begun to effect those great changes in human destiny which it is in their nature, and in their futurity to accomplish." Since these prophetic words were written, the movement which Mr. MILL foresaw has been commenced; the artisans of the country have secured one instalment of their share of the fruits of industry in the shape of a shortening of the hours of labour, and they are beginning to think that the time is approach- ing when they should secure another instal- ment. The . difficulty is as to how it has to be done; and for our own part we can- not help thinking, while admitting that the growing wealth of the world warrants the change, that application to Parliament, except in the case •of miners, should only be made as a last resort. It requires to be borne in mind that hitherto the working classes have been successful in gradually reducing the hours of labour without the help of the Legislature ; and what has been done in the past may be accomplished in the future. It is true that the shortening process has not extended to some classes of workers, and it might happen that these classes—the least organised—would be left .still further in the rear, if they were not helped by Parliament. It is this consideration which .gives strength to the agitation for providing, by means of an enactment, a weekly half-holiday for shop assistants. Events have shown that they are not in a position to enforce the boon by combina- tion amongst themselves, and that they are justi- fied in looking to Parliament to come to their rescue.

The most thoughtful and argumentative paper which we have yet seen on the subject of shorten- ing the hours of labour, appears in the December number of " The Westminster Review," with the title of" A plea for an eight hours day." The writer, Mr. Dion Ramsay, boldly confronts most of the difficulties which are raised by the question, and meets them with facts and figures which are, to say the least of them, entitled to consi- deration. He quotes from " Six Centuries of Work and Wages," by the late Mr. Thorold Rogers, to show that the lowest class of workers are, notwithstanding our enormous accummulation of wealth, in a more destitute and wretched condition of existence than were the serfs of the Middle Ages; and argues that what is needed to-day is not only a redistribution of wealth,but such a redistribution of leisure as would be afforded by an eight hours day. It is certainly , suggestive of what the struggle for existence means that, while "the average age at death amongst the wealthy classes, is fifty-five years, amongst the artisan classes of many of our large towns it is only thirty years." Another way of stating the same fact is to point out that the death-rate in some of the manufacturing towns is fifty per cent. higher than the death-rate of the country as a whole. There can be no question that ivorking shorter hours has a tendency to raise the standard of living; and that means adding to the average length of life. Mr. RAMSAY is not disturbed by the prediction that the eight hours day would mean a corres- ponding fall in wages, or, what might come to the same thing, a proportionate increase in the price of commodities. He argues that what would really happen would be that there would be less re- turn for capital ; in other words, that a fair share of the hundred and fifty millions of money which is every ) ear being added to tho wealth of the nation would remain in the hands of the workers, whose wages would not, therefore, need to be re- duced by reducing the hours of labour. Touching another point the writer says : Every social reformer knows that a rising of the standard of comfort, the spread of education, the opportunity for self-culture, and the diverse in- terests in life which increased leisure creates, act as a check upon the tendency to over-population, and that poverty, ign,orance, and degradation are the most prolific causes of a too-rapid multiplication of the species.

_ There is no gainsaying the truth of this statement, but it bears but indirectly on the safety and wisdom of the eight hours day. What politicians will wish to see, before they commit themselves to Nrliamentary enactment, is that the proposal will not seriously dislocate trade, or drive capital to other countries; that it is generally demanded by those whose interests are immediately affected; and that outside efforts as between employer and employed have proved of no avail.

THE ACTION ARISING FROM A DOG BITE. At St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday fore- noon, Deputy Judge Goldthorpe gave his decision in the claim by George Eccles, coal merchant, against William Atthur Duxbury, landlord of the Stanley Inn, Peasley Cross-lane, for damages arising out of the bite of a dog. The sum of £5O was claimed as damages, and the case was argued at the last sitting of the court. His Honour held that there was no evidence to show that the defen- dant was acquainted with the fact that the animal had bitten several persons, and under the circum- stances ho gave a verdict for the defendant, each party having to pay his own costs. Henry Burrows, 16 years of age, 1, Orrell-street, Parr, died on Saturday, under singular circum- stances. He was employed as a pony driver at Ashton's Green Colliery, and, on the morning of the 10th November, was in charge of a pony and some wagons of coal down the mine. One of the wagons got off the rails, and deceased afterwards told another workman that he had hurt his head in at- tempting to lift the wagon on to the rails again. He worked the remainder of the day, but was con- fined to bed on the following morning, when he be- came unconscious. Dr. Casey, and his assistant, Dr. Mills, were called in, but Burrows remained un- conscious almost up to his death. Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on the body of the deceased, at St. Helens, on Tuesday. Mr. T. Pennington, certificated manager of Ashton's Green Colliery, appeared on behalf of Messrs. Bromilow, Foster, and Co., by whom deceased was employed. Mr. T. Glover, miners' agent, was also present. Dr. Casey deposed that he attended deceased up to his death, and had that morning made a post-mortem examination, and found the symptoms of a severe congestion of the brain. That was the immediate cause of death, and might be brought on by a blow or severe pressure. John Burrows,deceased's father, stated that his son had stated he had hurt his head when trying to push a wagon on the rails with his bead. After further evidence, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." Hop WATER ITEATING.—GarIand sends estimates free. Warrington.—A /yr. WOMAN. why work so hard,? ' SUNLIGHT SOAP" does that. There has been a good deal said about Sitting Bull and his amiable friends rising—not to make speeches, but to relieve Americans of their scalps. Happily the settlers have up to now been allowed to keep their hair on; and in a little while, when troops have been concentrated, we may hope to hear of another "13u11's" Run.

The Staffordshire journals give full reports of Mr. Thomas Morris's paper, at Dudley, on "Some causes of the crystallisation of iron." Considerable discussion followed, as the subject is a much- debated one ; but it is hardly necessary to say that Mr. Morris, who has unrivalled experience, held his own at the South Staffordshire Institute.

Mr. George Eccleston, of Peasley Cross, does not get the £,50 which he claimed for loss of work, doctor's expenses, &c., incurred by being bitten by a dog. The St. Helens County Court Judge has ruled, in accordance with precedent, that, as no proof is forthcoming that the owner knew the animal was ferocious. he cannot be heM responsible. Moral: "Let dogs delight to bark and bite "—so long as they keep it from their owners that they do it in a ferocious way.

The word" gentleman" has many meanings, and of late years it has come down in the world. Win. Hemmons, an Earlestown pork butcher, who was bound over to keep the peace at the Newton Ses- sions, on Saturday, described himself as a gent,le- man. But, as it transpired that he had folloiked up this designation of himself with offering to fight a policeman and pushing him in the chest, the con- clusion come to was that ho was anything but a gentle man. -- The City Clerks' Alliance have been memoralis- ing the Lord Mayor "to use his influence with the City business firms to induce them to discontinue the practice of employing so many German and other foreign clerks while thousands of English clerks are out of employment." But the Lord Mayor feels himself powerless. English clerks, if they would beat their German competitors, must meet them on their own ground; they must put more brains into their work.

-- - The Prussian Government are taking in hand the question of promoting Dr. Koch's cure for tuberculosis; and it is satisfactory to know that measures will be adopted for making • the remedy perfectly accessible to the poor. One gentleman has given a sum of no less than one million marks with that object. The remedy is to be made pub- lic under such conditions as will render imitation impossible. This is a necessary precaution. No- body wishes to see quacks palming upon the public something which is not the genuine article.

The stars in their courses are said to have fought against Sisera, and they certainly fought against the Liberal candidate in St. John's Ward, Warring- ton. As the Manchester Municipal elections have shown, the Home Rule crisis has for the moment sent wavcrers over to the Tory side; and it is the waverers, unfortunately, that determine elections. But in addition to being a Liberal, Mr. Loughlin was the recognised leader of the Nationalists in Warrington, 1 and, as he himself said, it would under the circumstances have been a miracle if he had secured the seat.

The Tories are, of course, jubilant, and some of them are trying to persuade themselves that they have a majority in the ward. Granted that neither party polled its full strength on the first of November, he must be a very verdant politician who thinks that the 197 extra votes which Mr. Hill obtained, were the suffrages of 197 Tories who were too indifferent to vote for him at the pr3vious contest. Leaders on both sides know better than that ; they know that the conversion of a minority of 38 into a majority of 177 is due, not to Mr. Hill's fitness, but to Mr. Parnell's un- fitness.

"Throw plenty of mud and some of it will stick" was the principle upon which the Tories acted in opposing Mr. Loughlin. It is the usual way with what Mr. Chamberlain calls "the party of gentlemen." Aldermen Harrison appealed to the electors to vote against Mr. Loughlin because he was "an alien in nationality," SLc. And this from a leader of the party which has so much to say about " Separation " ! Ireland must have no separate Government ; but Irishmen in this coun- try must be separated from other citizens—ex- cluded as "aliens in blood," &c. This is consis- tency—the consistency of Toryism.

The member for Newton made the most, on Saturday, of the Parnell difficulty at a meeting at Golborne. This was a matter of course; but we do not see that it was a matter of course to say that Mr. Gladstone had sought out Mr. Parnell for a " miserable purpose." If the purpose was miserable, what of the purpose of the late .Lord Carnarvon, who at an earlier date sought out and interviewed the Irish leader with Lori Salisbury's full knowledge ? In discassing this matter, Air. Legh will do well to take Dr. Johnson's advice and clear his mind of cant.

Di. Joseph Parker's love of the sensational makes him at times rash in his assertions. Preaching at the City Temple on Sunday,he said," Home Rure,as we bad known it, it was dead and gone, and nothing could revive it in this generation." There is surely a trace in this random statement of the madness which he attributes to Mr. Parnell. Home Rule has taken that hold upon the United Kingdom that it cannot die. It will live and it will flourish yet, not only in Ireland, but in England, in Scot- land, and in Wales.

Mr. Gladstone' at eighty, has not lost hears; it is not in him to despair. He is the hero of the hour; and he stands at this moment nearer to the hearts of his countrymen—Tory as well as Liberal —than he has ever done before. His letter to Mr. John Mellor, Q.C., the Liberal candidate for Bassetlaw, shows that in his judgment the struggle for Home Rule must go forward upon the old lines, even if the Irish have to choose a new leader. Mr. Parnell has ruined his reputation, but he has not ruined Home Rule. It may be deferred, but it is not dead.

There could be no harm in Alderman Davies warning the members of the Warrington Town Council, on Tuesday, that town improvements cannot be effected without money. But, if the improvements are 'real, the ratepayers will not grunible. They have settled on freeing the Library, and have themselves voted the money for the purpose. They are willing, too, to pay the price for better baths; and they wish to see the blackest of the Black Spots of Warrington speedily removed. The working-man's health is the work- ing-man's wealth, and it is true economy to protect it by providing well paved streets, yards, and passages, and by insisting on the closure being applied to houses unfit for human habitation.

Alderman Davies let the cat's head out of the bag when he said that they might shortly be asked' to subscribe or raise a sum of £5,000 for the put- poses of a Technical School; and the head being out the sooner the body and tail are seen the better. Blackburn has ,recently subscribed about £15,000 for a Technical School, and Warrington should be equal to providing one-third of that sum. Considering that at least £150,000 a year is de- voted to drinking-shops it is surely not too much to expect an odd E5,0d0 for one year to be set aside for a thinking-shop. Please, therefore, to hurry up, you gentlemen who have this matter in hand. Alderman Davies has given the cue.

It was suggested at the meeting of the Warring- ton Board of Guardians, on Wednesday, that in appointing a successor to the Rev. S. Wilkinson as chaplain to the Workhouse, a portion of the salary should be set aside for payment of the Roman Catholic priest who ministers to the Roman Catho- lic inmates. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton seemed to think this should be in the way of an additional payment, but that would mean putting a heavier tax on the ratepayers for the same work as hereto- fore. Let the Guardians decide, if they like, to allow something out of the £6O now paid to a 'Catholic priest, giving the bulk to the chaplain. We venture to predict that there will be no lack of applicants for the post.

On Tuesday orders were issued from the War Office for a new Volunteer Home Defence Brigade to be formed, to be designated the Cheshire and Lancashire Brigade, the corps comprising it being taken from the existing Mersey and Welsh Border • Brigades. The corps comprising the new brigade are those belonging to Bury, Rochdale, Salford, Stockport, Congleton Warrington, and St. Helens. The Manchester brigade, already consisting of lire battalions, has been increased to sixiby the addition of the Oldham battalion. The Mersey Brigade will in future consist of the six Liverpool and the one Birkenhead corps; and the Northern Counties Bri- gade of the lllverston, Blackburn, Burnley, Preston, Bolton, Cumberland, and the Mid-Westmorland corps. THE ACCIDENT AT FARNWORTH PARISH CHURCH, Mr. W. 'l'. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an in- quest at the Widnes Accident Hospital on Saturday, on the body of Richard Sothern, aged 62 years, of 12 Chats- worth-st., Liverpool. The deceased was one of a num- ber engaged fronting the roof of Farnworth Parish Church, on the 13th ult., and he fell from the scaffold, a distance of 20 feet,sustaining injuries from which he died on Thursday week. A verdi,ct of " Accidental Death " was returned. THE HORSE AMBULANCE FOR WIDNES.

The horse ambulance, for the construction of which the Police and Tradesmen's Cricket Club raised the necessary funds, has been completed by Mr. C. Tyrer, of West Derby-road, Liverpool. It is similar to the convey- ances supplied to surrounding towns, and is fitted up with every requisite for thc removal of patients with comfort and convenience. It is at present located at the police gtation, but a special place will be constructed for its reception at the Accident Hospital.

div.head: UNVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: UNVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.

The fifth of the series of lectures on political economy was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Thursday week. There was only a sparse attendance. Mr. H. Llewellyn Smith 8.A., B.Sc., the lecturer, dealt with "The prob- lem of poverty, and the wages question." He compared the wages of the past with those of the present time, and explained how the introduction of the steam engine and the power loom—" the industrial rovolution" —had given rise to the social problem in its present form.

div.head: MIDNIGHT MARAUDER AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A MIDNIGHT MARAUDER AT RUNCORN.

John Aston, a middle-aged man was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, charged with being found on the premises of Plicebe Dunn, stationer, Szc., Bridge-st. About midnight on Sunday, P.C. Edwards found the prisoner asleep on the floor of the shop, which is a " lock-up " establishment, and a plate glass window, by which the prisoner had evidently made his entrance, was broken.—The prisoner said he was drunk at the time and on promising to make good the damage estimated at£2 108. he was discharged. div.head: HONOURS TO A RUNCORN GENTLEMAN.
div.p: HONOURS TO A RUNCORN GENTLEMAN.

Our respected young townsman, Mr. Charles A. Tim- mins, of " Rockfield," at the annual competition of the Livorpool Photographic Society carried away the first prize for lantern slides, and his pictures were specially commended by the judges. The first prize for lantern slides is the most coveted amongst the 280 members ; and the competition this year was a very severe one, as the work shown was of such excellent merit that the judges awarded two medals for second prize. The award of the judges was very heartily received, the winner being very popular amongst the members.

_ At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, C. H. Cots- worth, contractor, Jubilee Hall, Formby, was summoned by Widnes Local Board, for laying out a passage of a less width tnan 10 feet and also with not making the altera- tions required in a notice served upon him by the Sur- veyor of the Widnes Local Board.—Mr. Squarey (in- structed by Messrs. Oppenheim and Malkin) prosecuted, and the defendant was represented by Mr. Willis Harper, who said to make the alteration now would involve an expenditure of £4O. _ TREAT TO RUNCORN WORKHOUSE CHILDREN. On Thursday afternoon, the pupils of the Grove House School, Runcorn (Mrs. Soulby), gave an entertainment to the children of the Workhouse. The children, who walked from Dutton in charge of the schoolmaster and schoolmistress, were about 50 in number, and they were much admired,as they walked through the town,for their clean and bright appearance. After the entertainment the children were provided with a dapital tea at Mr. Riley's cafe in Bridge-st., and subsequently they were conveyed back to the Workhouse in conveyances from Mr. Jackson's livery stables. Mr. S. Taylor, one of the guardians, generously defrayed the cost of the tea and coaches. In the evening Mrs. Soulby's pupils repeated the entertainment to a.crovrded audience in Bethesda School- room, and the entertainment realised upwards of £lO, which will be devoted to giving the Workhouse children a treat at Christmas. The programme was as follows : Pianoforte duet, " Blake's Grand March," the Misses Soulby and K. Harrison; cantata, "Father Christmas." the Singing Class; violin solo, Miss Harrison ,accompanist Miss K. Harrison. Nursery Rhymes: Hunting piece, Miss Unsworth ; Song, "Driven from Home." Miss B. Price; recitation, "The Village Blacksmith," Miss M. Bellamy ; pianoforte solo, "Scotch Airs," 'Miss Soulby; quartette, ' Cockles and Mussels," the Misses Harrison, Johnson, Cameron, and Judson; gavotte. "Louis XIII," Miss Timmins; Tableaux vivants ; "The National Anthem." The entertainment was of an enjoyable character and the audience frequently encored the youth- ful performers. • DEATH OF A CHESHIRE HIGH BAILIFF. div.head: STnricm OF CoLLizas.
div.p: STnricm OF CoLLizas.

On Wednesday, the 100 colliers employed by the Eccleston Hall Collieries Company at their Gillen' Green pit, Eceleston, near St. Helene. came out on strike against an alteration of the rates of payment by the employers. The pit was started about twelve months ago, and since that time the men have been paid day wages. A fortnight since the firm inti- mated that in future they would be paid on piece- work terms, but the men declined to continue on those conditions, and the pit was stopped for one day. Mr. Thomas Glover, miners' agent, had an in- terview with the firm, and it was arranged that the hands should serve a fortnight's notice. The notice I expired on Wednesday, and on Tuesday Mr. Glover again waited upon the firm, who offered to pay the men 3s. 6d. per day. The demands of the colliers were to be paid ss. per day, and, as the firm would not accede to the wishes of the men, the latter brought out their tools and ceased work on Wednes- day afternoon.

£1,600 LOST. At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Deputy Judge Goldthorpe was occupied for several hours in hearing an interpleader case in regard to honsehold furniture, valued at about £53, and in which Mrs. Margaret Ann Harwood was the claim- :.ant, her husband, Ralph Harwood, the execution idebtor, and Messrs. E. Webster and Son, wine and ispirit merchants, the execution creditors. Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the claimant, and Mr. Hor- ' , ridge barrister, Liverpool, (instructed by Mr. W. Webster) represented the execution creditors. Mr, 'Riley stated on behalf of Mrs. Harwood that she had • received two legacies—one of £490 and another of £soo—out of which the furniture was purchased, though some of the receipts appeared in her hus- band'sname. During the last three years she had given him money, until the whole of the £l,OOO had gone. He had been unfortunate in business. The defence was that the claimant bad acted in a way which led the creditors to think the goods belonged to her husband.—His Honour, while expressing sympathy with the creditors, said Mrs. Harwood had told a consistent story, and he gave judgment for the claimant of the goods with costs.
UMBRELLAS ItE-covF.asm at the shortest notice.—J. & W. Durrox's Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. A CHAPTER. Car ACCIDENTS.

On Monday evening, as a party of gentlemen were passing in a conveyance through Croft, they met with what might have proved to be a serious acci- dent. It appears that the party were Mr. James Daxon, of Orchard Farm, Culchetb (whose wife had been buried that afternoon), his cousins Mr. James and Mr. William Hunt, of Croft, and a lady friend from Warrington. The horse was Mr. Daxon's, and the conveyance Mr. W. Hunt's. When they had got to the Smithy-lane end the shafts broke, and the occupants were thrown on the road, the trap being dragged several yards. Alight was it once procured, and assistance rendered, after which the horse was taken home and the conveyance left at the cottage until morning. Happily none of the occupants were the worse for their accident. Shortly after another accident occurred near the same Place. A number of gentlemen were returning from Warrington fair in Mr. Thomas Welsby's conveyance, he being one of the partv, when, on turning the corner of the end of Smithy-lane into the New-road on their way home, the horse ran up the bank, and was thrown over. The occupants fell on to the road though happily none of them were hurt. On Sat- urday afternoon a serious accident occurred to a young man named William Collier, son of John Collier, of Lord-street, Croft. It appears that Col- lier, who is a labourer at the Vulcan Foundry, took a walk up to what is known Bathe Church fields in the afternoon, and commenced cutting a stick out of the hedge, when his knife suppled, and penetra- ted one of his knees. The wound bled profusely. Remedies were applied on his return home, and eventually Dr. Pattison, of Newton, the medical officer of the works, attended the unfortunate man, and on Tuesday morning he ordered him to be taken to the Warrington Infirmary. The Local Government -Board wrote in answer to an inquiry from the Authority, stating that they were not yet in a position to communicate their views upon the subiect of the Authority's application to take proceed- ingsagainst Messrs. W. R. Earp and Co., in respect to the pollution of gekewick Brook.—The Chairman: They are a long while about it. vaa WATER SUPPLY OF wEsvow,

A letter was read from ii;l3-Local Government Board with reference to the water supplies of Frodsham, He's- by, Dutton, Halton Common, Norley, and parts of Bar- tington, Budworth, and Clifton. The Board stated that theywould look to the Medical Officer of Health's report for the current year for an account of the progress made in obtaining water supplies for these places.—ln reply to Mr. Brandreth the Chairman said the Authority had given Frodsham Water Company notice to provide Frodsham with water, and if they did not do so, the Authority could find the water themselves.—Mr. Aaron said at Weston they had to pay the Water Company for water, and could not get any water.—The Clerk: The Westog people ought to look to that-The Chairman: It is a strange state of affairs.—Mr. Aaron said he continually received complaints from people, some days they were hours and could not get a toothful.- The Chairman: You ought to complain to the company.—Mr. Aaron : I have complained to the secretary and the chairman of the company. He wished an answer to this point. This Authority compels people to have a good and sufficient supply of water to their houses. We have not got water at Weston. We have to pay for it, and the Waterworks Company won't supply us.—The Clerk: It is entirely between the Waterworks Company and the people who pay.—Mr. Aaron: Has this Authority any power in the matter ?—The Clerk : No.—The Deputy Clerk : We compel people to supply themselves.—Mr. Aaron: The law on the subject is like a good many others, not worth 2d. (Laughter.)

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. Taylor, A. Salkeld, and G. Moss (clerk). •
, NEW APPOINTMENT. On the recommendation of the School Manage- ment Committee, Miss Annie Perkins was appointed assistant mistress at the Greenway-road girls school at a salary of £45 per annum. '

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE .
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE .

--- The School Attendance Committee reported that 60 parents had been summoned to appear before the Com- mittee for contravention of the Education Act • 63 appeared and were dealt with,l3 were prosecuted before, and convicted by the magistrates. Attendance Officer Bowyer reported that the attendance' at the elementary schools for the past month showed an improvement on the corresponding period of last year.—Dr. Gesteldi moved the adoption of the minutes and referred with gratifica- tion to the fact that the percentage of attendance had increased by three. There was a great disparity in the average attendance at the different schools and even in the different departments. He did not know whether it was to be attributed to work of the individual officers, or there was any kind of neglect on the part of the teachers connected with the specific echools.—Mr. Moss said the boys attended much better than the girls, and, infants attended badly in the winter months. The per- centage of attendance was neither better nor worse than the past few yeers. Last year there was an epidemic of measles adversely affected the attendance at school.— After some discussion Dr. Gastaldi said the work of the Committee was to important that he felt inclined to move that it consist of the whole Board.—Dr. McDougall

div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday morning. Mr. S. Taylor presided, and there present Messrs. J. Pritchard, W. Fisher, IL J. Grice, W. Lightburn, W. Mellor, W. Timmins, R. Abel, J. lEVBR IN TIM TOWN. The Medical Officer (Dr. McDougall) reported that the number of deaths registered during November amounted to 31 ; of these 2 were inquest cases and of the remain- ing 29 deaths, 8 were due to bronchitis, 5 to pthisis, 2 to imperfect respiration, 2to apoplexy, 2to paralysis, 4 to the zymotic class of disease, and one each to kidney disease, epilepsy, heat disease, syncope, softening of the brain, and one to old age. The 31 deaths showed an average death rate for the 12 months of 20.8 and exclu- sive of the inquest cases of 19.3.—Mr. Lightburn said the local paper (the" Examiner ") had stated there were 50 cases of typhoid fever, in Dukes Field District, and lie asked the Medical Officer if this were a fact.—Dr. McDougall replied that he could not answers any ques- tion unless he looked at documents in his possession. I Statements of a very wide character have been made.— Mr. Lightburn said writers in newspapers ought to be I sure of their facts before creating a public scare.—Mr. Imiscn : It is a notorious fact that writers in news- papers never are sure of their facts. (Lsughter.) Mr. Lightburn : We must endeavour to make them as ac- curate as we can. • HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS This Committee recommended that the application of Messrs. Balfours and Co., Limited, of London, for per- mission to fix automatic delivery machines for the sale of postage stamps and cards, in close proximity to post offices, pillar and wall boxes and other spots convenient to the public, be granted, subject to the exact site of each machine being indicated by the Surveyor, and to an acknowledgment of is. being made for each machine annually. That a 24inch pipe sower be made from a point marked A on the plan submitted (near Union-st.), along Heath-road to a point marked B near the Victoria- road Viaduct, and that tenders be obtained for the cut- ting and laying of the sewer, and for the supply of the sewer pipes. div.head: HOSPITAL FREE.

That the sum of 12s. be remitted to Charles Osmond for the maintenance of his son Edward in the hospital—me Lightburn moved the acceptance of the minutes, and referring to the last re- commendation, said the hospital was tree, except for those who could afford to pay. Although they wanted to make the hospital as widely useful as possible, times- should have some consideration for the rates, and he thought no man would contend that the ratepayers should pay for people who were able to pay for them- selves. (sear, hear.)—Mr. Fisher seconded the motion. —Mr. Smith said in this instance it was a very deserving case.

div.head: FiwAs-cn.
div.p: FiwAs-cn.

The report of the Finance Committee, which was re- ceived on the motion of Mr. Imison, stated that the receipts on genenal fund were £366 93. 5d., loan account £l,OOO, and Library fund £52 10s. 9d. Accounts amounting to £382 2s. 6d. on general account, aid £530 is. 2d. on loan account were passed for payment. The balance in the treasurer's hands amounted to £2,428 17s. 3d. The balance to be collected on general district rate was £2,154 4s. od.—The Committee recommended that the rent charged ta Mr. Samuel Crosby for land near Waterloo Bridge be reduced from £27 to £l5 per annum, in consequence of the closing of the cottage and weighing machineund the reduction of the space available for the coalyard. • TRH PRES LIBRARY—IMPORTANT DISCUSSION. The Library Committee recommended that the Board of Commissioners be recommended from the end of the pre- sent financial year to grant the Library Committee the use of Library and reading room premises free &Obi the payment of rent —Mr. Once moved the adoption of the minute in order that it might be discussed. He thought Mr. Humphreys, who moved the resolution, would have been present.—Mr. Hankinson seconded for the same reason, and said at the meeting of the Committee it was not shown that they were impoverished in funds, and Mr. Humphreys gave no bona fide reason why the rent should be remitted. On that ground he did not support it at all.—ln answer to Mr. Once, the Law Clerk said he thought,the Commissionershad power to grant the Library Committee the use of rooms over and 'above the penny rate, but they would have to obtain the consent of the Treasurer —Mr. Smith moved the rejection of the minute. He argued that the payment of £3B a year was a trivial matter as it included heating, 'lighting and cleaning, and there were other matters equally as pressing await- ing the consideration of the Board and Finance Com- mittee to spend money.—Mr. Lig,htburn said any pro- posal affecting the education or intelligence of the people was always a great temptation to that and other Boards, which had the interest of the inhabitants at heart, but with thattemptation there was a corresponding duty and that was to take care that the money of the ratepaysrs was properly spent. He contended that the Library reports were against the recommendation entirely, show- ing that in the year ended in June of the present year, there were only 18 more borrowers than in the previous year, while the number of books lent was something like g 72 less. There was an increasing encroachment upon the money reserved for town's affairs and the Commis- sioners ought to take care of the leakages here and there.—Mr. Meadowcroft expressed regret at the absence of Mr. Humphreys, and went on to point out the rent included gas, heating and cleaning, as well as accom- modation, and he was of opinion that already the Library Committee had their premises practically free from rent. The Commissioners had also borrowed money to improve the premises and the Committee were relieved of the interest on that money. The question was were the Commissioners justified in foregoing this charge of rent. He was strongly of opinion that under the Libraries Act they had any such power. What seemed to him extra- ordinary was that a gentleman who was connected with the Library should have stated that there was only something like £5O a year to spend in books. He had gone through the accounts of the Library since the year 1882, and he found that they had had considerable balances—that in fact they had boen unable to spend all the money they had received. Not until a year ago did they reduce that balance, and that was on account of an intimation which they received from the auditor that they had no right to have this balance in hand. When they found that they could not accumulate money, they spent away as hard as they could, whether judicially or not,he was not prepared to say, and reduced the balance practically to nothing. In 1890 the income of tho Corn- mitte was £230, and after paying the rent they had £2OO to spend on the Library. He thought they had ample funds, and that the Library was as well equipped as any Library of its size in the kingdom, and they had sufficient money to carry on the Library efficiently and satisfactorily.—Mr. Pritchard referred with pleasure to the fact that the Library was a useful institution, and much appreciatod, but said he believed in every depart- ment bearing its fair share of the financial burdens be- longing to it, and he believed that the Library did not do more than pay its fair propo:tion. He was not at all satisfied with the present position of the Free Library and reading-room. To be neglectesito the back premises of the establishment like that, and ap- proached by a side entrance in a second-rate street was not at all creditable for a community of their size and if the Committee would give their attention to providing a home for the library—and it is rumoured that benevo-

lent gentlemen are prepared to assist in an object like that—that would be both a more worthy object for the c3nsideratioa of the Committee, and something of far greater importance might becomeof it than the remission of the rent now sought for.—The Chairman said no one sympathised with the object of the Library more than he did, and he was pleased that advantage was taken of the facilities offered to the public, but he must oppose this minute. They must not lose sight of the financial ques- tion. There were many projects desirable, but they could not be carried out without money,and if the Board did not mind they would in March have something fac- ing them which would not be very agreeable to the rate- payers. Last year they succeeded with very great diffichlty in keeping the rate at 2s. 2d. but he could see dearly that if they did not mind 2s. 4d. in the £ would not clear them for the next year. The Library was in a fair position, and he did not see the necessity, under the eiretfifistances,of remittting the rest.—Mr. Imison agreed with Mr. Pritchard that the present Library building was unsuitable and if the Committee could get the it'..o.operation of outsiders and _were able to establish a more suitable building in the immediate neighbour- hood,. that would be a better course for them to take. ' There was no doubt the increasing work of that Board would demand in a short time that those rooms should be available for the purpose of the Commissioners; and, therefore, the question might as well be faced now as in a short time, and the Committee should think seriously about making provision for themselves.—Mr. Pritchard said no doubt the Commissioners would give them every reasonable help.—Mr. Grice having spoken against the resolution, it was unanimously rejected.

TECHNICAL EDUCATION. The Secretary read the following letter: "The Mount, Higher Runcorn, 11th November, 1890.—Dear Sir, I have pleasure in informing you that the County Council of Cheshire on Friday last elected me a member of the Technical Education Committee for the Urban Authority of Runcorn. My colleagues on the Commis- sioners' Board can rely upon me doing my best in the interests of Runcorn.—Yours faithfully, P. Speak- man."

TES MYDIT.-HELVT SURCHARGE. The secretary said the auditorhad reported as follows: —"I do hereby certify that in these accounts of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners for the year ended at Lady Day, 1890,! have disallowed the Sums of £lOO, 4s. 2d., and 55., as payments illek ally made out of the funds of the said Board of Commissioners, and I find that Mr. Edward Imison, of Runcorn, authorised the making of the said illegal payments of £lOO and 4s. 2d., and I do hereby surcharge him with the same; end I hereby find that Mr. J. W. Lightburn,of Runcorn, autho- rised the said payment of 55., and I do hereby surcharge him with the same. (Signed) Alfred W. Dolby, assistant auditor." In giving his reasons for these surcharges, the auditor said the sum of £lOO was entered as paid to Messrs. F. and G. Holme, engineers, for services alleged to have been rendered by them in connection with the I proposed improvement of Waterloo Bridge, and he dis- allowed the amount because there were no particulars produced either to the Commissioners or to him at the audit, showing how the amount of £lOO had been ar- rived at; and in the absence of such par- ticulars he was unable to say whenever or to what extent the sum was reasonably or lawfully incurred and due to the said engineer, because so far as he was able to judge, the services in respect of which the said sum was paid, were rendered more than six months prior to the making of the district rate upon which the said sum ultimately became a charge, and therefore the said sum was paid and charged upon tbe funds of the Commissioners without lawful authority. As to the sum of 4s. 2d., this was part of a sum of £l6 13s. 4d. paid to the . secretary as increased salary at the rate of £2OO per annum, for the month of April, 1889, and he disallowed the sum of 4s. 2d. because the Salary of the secretary was not increased by the Commissioners front £175 to £2OO per annum until April 4th, and the said sum of 4s. 2d. (increased salary from April Ist to 3rd) was not legally due to or recoverable by the secretary, and the same was unlawfully paid to him and charged in the account of the Commis;loners. With regard to the sum of 55., this was entered and charged as paid to the Cheshire constabulary in respect of service,' rendered by a police constable in preserving order on the fair ground on bank holiday, and he disallowed the ' amount Lecause the duty of keeping the peace was not a duty cast upon the said Commissioners either by the Public Health Act, or the Runcorn Improvement Acts, or otherwise, and the said sum was not lawfully payable by or recoverable from the Commissioners, or a legal charge upon the funds under their control. BATHS. _

After some discussion On---;-proposition made by Mr. Smith, a deputation of four members were authorised to accompany the Surveyor to inspect the baths at North- wich, reasonable expenses to be paid by the Board.

IMPORTANT NOTICE. Mr. Meadowcroft gave notice that at the next meeting he should move that this Board does not put into oper- ation the powers of the Technical Education Act until the School Board are able to provide intermediate or secondary education for the middle class of the town.
TIELNGS HEARD AND SEEN AT -RUNCORN, &c.

BY "AN OCCASIONAL COMIRSPONDENT." That the return of attendances of the members of Cheshire County Council shows that Mr. Speakman, the representative for Runcorn South, has attended 56 meetings, and Major Ilazlehurst, the elect of Runcorn North, has only put in an appearance at eight meetings. That it is highly probable that Mr. Thomas Snape, C.C., of Widnes and Liverpool, will be selected to contest the Southerly Division of Yorkshire in the Liberal interest at the next election, in place of the present, representative, Mr. E. Crossley, who is re- tiring. That the people of Runcorn will be glad to know that the hospital is "practically free," only those who can afford to pay being charged the fees of the establishment.

That the fees of one patient were remitted at the meeting on Thursday. That typhoid fever is still prevalent in the town, but has considerably abated within the past two weeks, and during the past month there were four deaths from zymotic causes. That at the meeting of the Board of Commis.. sioners, on Thursday, the Free Library Committee practically got notice to quit and finds home for the institution elsewhere, because their premises would be required by the increasing work of the Board.
That should the Board adopt the Technical Edu- cation Act—and it is to be hoped they will—the Technical School of the Free Library might with advantage be placed under the same roof.

div.p: FRODSHAM.

div.p: LYIIII.

div.head: 130LTON MURDER.
div.p: THE 130LTON MURDER.

Among the many sorrowful features of the murder of the poor young woman Holt of Longworth, near Bolton, it is stated that her unhappy mother was in great measure dependent upon her for support. A Committee has been formed for raising a fund for her assistance. It consists of the Mayor of Bolton, the Vicar of Walmsley, the minister of the Unitarian, Chapel, Walmsley ; the minister of the Congregational Church, Egerton; and several other gentlemen of position and influence in the. neighbourhood.

div.p: WAGES IN THE BUILDING TRADE.

THE SEWERAGE OF RUNCORN. In the Chancery Division of the High Court of Jus- tice, yesterday, before Mr. Justice North, the Guar- dians of the Runcorn Union renewed their motion to restrain the Manchester Ship Canal Company, uutil the trial or further order, from entering upon or interfering with the sewage works under the con- trol of the Guardians until the defendants bid, in compliance with Sec. 76 of the Manchester. Ship Canal Act of 1885. provided at their own expense and to the reasonable satisfaction of the Guardians, other proper or sufficient sewers, outfalls, and works His Lordship granted the injunction.

div.head: WORKtIOITS FIRE.-SIX LIVES LOST.
div.p: WORKtIOITS FIRE.-SIX LIVES LOST.

Early on Thursday morning it was discovered that fire had broken out in one of the wards of the workhouse at Newcastle-under-Lyme. The inmates were roused, and most of them escaped at once from the burning building. Five old women had a small sitting-room to themselves at one end of the wing, and three of them were either suffocated by the smoke or killed by the fall of the building. One woman who escaped left behind her a boy, aged three years who usually slept with her, and he was burned to death. A young woman named Meakin, whose duty it was to light •the fires in the ward each morning, was also killed,ami another woman, named Burroughes, after making Ler way to a place of safety, was so affected by the fright and the smoke that she expired. The cause of the fire has net been ascer- tained, but it is surmised that Meakin, while lighting the fires as usual, accidentally set fire to the stock of chips kept in one of the cupboards.

div.head: NEVER OLD WHEN THE HEART IS
div.p: NEVER OLD WHEN THE HEART IS
YOUNG.
There is sound sense and reason in the saying that "
an is always just the age of his heart." That is to say
a man may be young, as years go, and old in feeling. He
may be lacking in hope, ambition and energy, and there-

fore to all intents and purpose to be an old man. On the other hand he may be seventy years of age, and still so full of vigour and elasticity that he is worth a dozen men who haven't been half as long in the world as he has. What a pity it is that people do not know how to avoid the causes which make them old and feeble before their time. We cite a case—one out of thousands.

Mrs. Mary Cuddy, of No. 23, Catherine-st., Richmond- road, Leeds, recently told to a friend the story of her life, and among other things she said: "Ever since I was a girl I have suffered from illness. I always had a pain both before and after eating, and never seemed able to gain and keep my strength ; a.ad felt that something was pulling me down. I had a nasty, queer sinking feel- ing in my stomach. Sometimes food seemed to ease it, and at other times it made me feel worse. Commonly when food was placed before me I could not touch it, and I often fainted at the very siybt of it. After a while I became so weak I could scarcely stand or walk. I thought it was consumption coming on by degrees, and I took all sorts of things to try and get relief, but it was no use.

" With the weakness and the loss of appetite there were other feelings and signs that were bad, and alarmed me greatly. Among them were these: A yellowish colour of the skin and eyes, sometimes a cold and clam- my perspiration, pains and aches in the sides, chest and back, headache, a kind of wind or gas coming up into my throat and mouth that was so sour and sickening I could scarcely bear it ; once in a while I would have a strange fluttering and palpitation that made me think my heart must be affected. I always slept badly, and frequently had horrible dreams, and was so melancholy and depressed in spirits that I got little or no pleasure 'as time dragged wearily by. I had so little energy or strength. that it was all I could do to summon courage for the labour upon which the family, at least in part, depended for support. lam a dressmaker, and you can fancy how hard my life must have been, and I didn't think it would last much longer.

"Not long ago I made up my mind to try a medicine that you are aware is advertised and known all over the country. I mean Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I had , no faith in it, of course, at first; for how can one believe I in what one knows nothing about? I bought and tried Mother Seigel's Curative Symp only because of its repu- tation. How could so many people, I asked myself praise a medicine so much if it had no virtue? I can only say I found what they said to be true. After begin- ning with the Syrup relief soon followed. My food digested better and gave me strength; and by persevering with it all my pains disappeared. I could eat my food with a relish and everything agreed with me. Now and then, when, through confinement and hard work, I have an occasional turn of my old complaint, I take a dose or two of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup,' and the trouble goes no further." _ _

Mrs. Caddy's ailment was indigestion and dyspepsia, and the palpitation of the heart that worried her returned no more after the function of digestion went on properly and naturally. The reason is th't the unusual action of the heart was caused by the pressure against it of the stomach, when the latter was filled with the gas gener- ated by the fermented food.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

THURSDAY.—Before his Honor Judge Ffoulkes. THE CAUSE LlST.—This list comprised 5 ad- journed plaints, 2 default summonses, 149 original plaint summonses, 35 judgment summonses, and 4 adjourned judgment summonses. THE RESPONSIBILITIES OF TENANTS.—WiIIiam Coates, Friars'-green, wholesale draper, sued John Dixon, Vene- tian blind manufacturer, for 155., being 3s. for one week's rent of a warehouse occupied by the defendant, and 12s. for windows repaired, after the defendant had left the premises. A counter-claim had been filed for 16s. 3d. for storing a piece of timber, at 3d. per week. Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiff. His Honour, after hearing the evidence gave a verdict for the plaintiff on the claim. The counter-claim was then gone into. Defendant admitted that he would not have sued for the 16s. 3d. if Mr. Coates had not charged him for the win- dows. His Honor said that, inasmuch as defendant had made no special contract to charge for the storage of the timber, and as he had admitted he would not have charged had not Mr. Coates put him in court for the broken windows, he could not recover the amount. It was a well-known rule of law that all tenants were bound to keep their tenements in proper order. The rule in- cluded the putting in of broken windows, whether broken accidently or otherwise. He therefore gave judgment for the plaintiff on the claim and counter-claim. THE CLAIM OF A WARRINGTON DOCTOR.—Robert W. Jack, surgeon, Church-st.,Warrington, brought an action against the trustees of the English Industrial Friendly Society, 130, Duke-st., Liverpool. Plaintiff sought pay- ment of a sum of £5 7s. 2d., claimed as one quarter's salary as medical officer of the society for the district of Warrington. The defendant society counter-claimed for £l5, made up as follows :—Damages claimed from the plaintiff for a breach of contract in not carrying out his agreement as medical officer, £5 ; and £lO claimed because the plaintiff " conspired with „Li.e.wry John Lyons to injure the def...aantsociety, and to trans- fer, and did with the assistance of the before-mentioned persons transfer, and induce many of the members of the defendant society to leave the said society, and to become members of a rival society of which , the plaintiff was physician and surgeon while he (the plaintiff) was in the employ of the defendants. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Quilliam, solicitor, Liverpool, appeared for the defend- ant society.—Mr. Browne, after stating the facts of the case, asked that the defendant society's solicitor should give the name of the rival society mentioned in the counter-claim, and his Honour ruling that the solicitor was bound to do so, Mr. Quilliam said that the society was called the Local Medical Aid Society. Dr. Jack was the physician of it, and the two men, Leigh and Lyons, were the factotums.—Plaintiff then gave evidence in support of his claim. He was, he said, appointed medi- cal officer of the English Industrial Friendly Society in 1888, at a remuneration of 7s. per annum for each family, and 2s. 6d. per annum for each member. He should remain the medical officer until Christ- mas next. He denied having ever refused to attend any patient. He sent in notice of his resignation I on the 29th of September. He admitted, in cross- examination, that on the 30th of August he resigned his position as medical officer. He insisted upon his resig- nation because he had failed to get any salary. After I consulting his solicitor he gave three months' notice.' Early in October,Lyons asked him to visit some members of the Aid Society, and to send in the bills to him. He had since attended two or three patients a week who were members of the Aid Society. He was not aware when that society came into existence when he sent in his resignation.—ln reply to Mr. Browne,witness said that he I had nothing to do with forming the new society.—Mr. ' Quilliam contended that the doctor had broken or at- tempted to break, his contract with the defendant soeiety, and that therefore he could not now sue. He had no right to go and leave the society in the lurch .—His Honour said that the notice was quarterly, and the salary should be paid quarterly. A resignation could not terminate such a contract, however much the plaintiff might have insisted upon it. To do so was waste of time without the other side assented.—Mr. Quilliarn, after some further conversation withdrew the counter-claim with a view of possibly taking action against Leigh and Lyons, in ' another court.; lint submitted that therewas no evidence to enable the plaintiff to arrive at the figures of his claim. He also questioned Leigh, who was called as a witness, and who said that he and Lyons constituted the new society. They collected money, paid the medical officer, and kept the balance. It was after they had concluded to conduct a medical society that they got the services of the plaintiff. Witness did not transfer any members of the new society. He was formerly a member I of the defendant society.—His Honour: That is not an unlawful thing to do.—After hearing various witnesses,his Honour said that there was no evidence of unlawful conspiracy, nor was he satisfied that at any time the plaintiff refused to attend patients. He should give judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed, with costs.—Mr. Browne asked for an immediate order as to the costs, and called Mr. Lyons as a witness in support of the application. This witness said that he was formerly a member of the committee of the defendant society, and was proceeding to give evidence as to the funds ot the society, when his Honour said there was nothing in that. The funds of such societies werefiuctuating. He allowed the usual time for payment.

WARRINGTON RECS. NJ-T.:JOE -COAT RANGEIZS.—The Blue Coat Rangers put in an appearance at Sankey on Saturday, and were beaten by 6 tries and 4 minors 'to nil.

WARRINGTON RECS. V. BLUE COAT RANGERS.—The Blue Coat Rangers put in an appearance at Sankey on Satur- day, but minus several of their leading players, the Rangers being beaten by 6 tries and 4 minors to nil. WARRINGTON V. OLDHAM.—This match, which was to have played at Oldham on Saturday. was abandoned owing to the frost. A similar fate, it will be remem- bered, awaited last season's engagement. The match between the " A " teams was also cancelled, the ground at Wilderspool being totally unfit for football pur- poses. .

ORFORD RANGERS V. RUNCORN JOCKEYS.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday. After some hard play by both teams, Bramwood got a try for the home team failing at goal. A few minutes grand play having followed, Rutter got a second try for the home team, a goal resulting, half time being called with the home team 1 goal 1 try, visitors nil. The visiters kicked off and after some hard play the game resulted—Orford Rangers 1 goal, 1 try, 2 miners ; Run- corn, 2 minors. WARRINGTON STAR V. WIDNES VICTORIA.—This match was played on the ground of the fernier on Saturday last. Neither team was fully represented, and owing to the severe frost the ground was in a hard condition. Harris kicked off on behalf of the home team, and after a spell of even play the visitors scored an unimproved try. Just before half time W. Makin scored for the home team, Newey making a grand bid for goal. The visitors restarted and the Stars at once attacked, and Barratt made a grand run in for the home team, Newey kicking a splendid goal. From now to the call of time the Stars had all the best of the game, beating their opponents at all points. Jackson and Morris again scored tries leav- ing the Stars victorious by 1 goal, 3 tries, 3 minors to Widnes Victoria 1 try and 1 minor. Star team : Full back, J. Harris; three-quarter backs, IV. Barratt (cap- tain), W. Clare, G. Jackson; half backs, IV. Morris and E. Rowlands; forwards, Newey, W. Makin, J. Urinston, Holden, Plumpton, Harding, Whittaker, T. Makin.
