HOUSE OF COMMONS, MONDAY.

The Deputy Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. Imsa LAND LEOISLATION.—Mr. Rathbone, who was but indistinctly heard in the gallery, gave notice of an amendment to the motion for the second reading of the Irish Land Bill, to the effect that the creation of a class of owners other than bona fide peasant proprietors would tend to aggravate the existing agrarian difficulty in Ire- land, a difficulty which might be thereby extended to other parts of the United Kingdom. THE LAND PURCHASE ACT.—Mr. BeLvoun, in reply to Mr. Shaw Lefevre said that up to the 31st October last the Land Commission had refused to make advances under the Land Purchase Act, 1885, in 2,500 cases, on the ground that there was not sufficient security for the amount applied for. ETHER DRINKING 1/4 IRELAND.—Mr. dOSCHEN replying to Dr. Cameron, said that in consequence of the use of ether as an intoxicant—sometimes with fatal results—in 'South Derry and Tyrone, an order of the Lord-Lieutenant in Council had been issued scheduling it as a poison, in which form only it could iniuture be sold. THE TITHES BILL.

Sir M. H. BEACH moved the second reading of the Tithes Bill, and said its object was solely to secure the better payment of tithe, and so to prevent the loss of a valuable property. The measure contained no provision relating to redemption, but a commission would be ap- pointed to consider that point. Under the present Bill tithe-owners would be pre vented from contracting them- selves out of the payment of tithes, but they would have a remedy against the landowner instead of against the tenant. Where the owner was the occupier of the land distraint could be retained under the Tithes Act only by County Court officers. The desire of the Government in introducing this measure was to amend the law, which in his (Sir Michael's) opinion was too long delayed. Mr. H. GARDNER said the proposed measure was very incomplete, and only touched the fringe of the question. _

Mr. C. W. GRAY Supported the second reading. Mr. Prarorr said the Bill was considerably superior to anything the Government had previously submitted. Mr. RENDEL moved an amendment to the effect that no tithe measure would be satisfactory to the people of Wales if it did not recognize the fact that tithes were national property, and that it should be applied in accord- ance with the wishes of the Welsh people. The discussion was continued by, amongst others, Mr. 0. Morgan, Mr. Cornwallis West, Mr. Byron Reed, and Mr. Bryn Roberts. The Bill was eventually read a second time. The House adjourned at 11.45. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL -RUGBY.
As in many other places the matches in Runcorn and Widnes districts were on Saturday abandoned in conse- quence of frost.

For once in a way football form received a confirma- tion in the graat match at Whalley Range on Saturday. Those who had carefully followed the doings of the Lancashire and Yorkshire fifteens in their preliminary engagements could arrive at one conclusion only, and that was that the probabilities were largely in favour of the County Palatine coming off victoriously. And so it proved. Even the Yorkshiremen themselves expected it although they would not admit it, or why bring so much pressnre to bear on Bonsor to fill one of the weak spots in their ranks ? They knew that Lancashire had at their command the best back division they had turned out for years, and it was this that made them particularly uneasy as to the result. It was here where the great strength of Lancashire lay, and it was this advantage that carried the day and placed the balance of wins to their credit once again.

Almost up to the very last there were grave doubts about the match being played owing to the severity of the weather at the end of the week. Thanks, however, to the foresight of the authorities, the ground had been well protected for some days, and when the covering was removed it was found to be in very good order. It was, doubtless, the uncertainty about the fixture being brought off that caused the discreditable scenes at the entrances to the enclosure. The bulk of the spectators seemed to rush up in a body almost at the last moment, and so many sought admission together, that the means of entry were totally mad'

,'. The patience of the ;-eridOus crowd soon became exhausted, and many hundreds mounted the pailings on different sides of the field, scores of pounds being thus lost, besides the damage to the fencing. Some of the players even were obliged to scale the boards, and altogether the scene was to be regretted in every way. The arrangements for such a big gathering were sadly at fault.

There is much more pleasure in speaking of the game itself. Had it not been for the unlucky mishap to Maw- son in the first few minutes, which deprived Yorkshire of the services of their full back, the football would have been thoroughly enjoyed. It was a capital display, and never approached weariness. For a time the visitors were very aggressive indeed, and although the forwards were a man fewer than their opponents they fully held their own. Lancashire seemed unable to break away, and when at length James Naylor scored the first try, the Yorkshire supporters present did not forget to cheer. There was nothing special about the try, andJowett had no chance of turning it into a premier point. Up to the interval Lancashire did little in the shape of attack, but a vast change was witnessed very soon after the teams got to work again, and for something like three-fourths of the second half Yorkshire had no rest at all. The home forwards were now terribly in earnest, and almost rushed their more bulky rivals off their feet. The backs tackled with determination and passed most unselfishly, and in the end Lancashire were the victors by two goals and a try to a try.

Yorkshire can, and will, of course, find an excuse in the early loss of Alawson. They had not only to play a man short, but the post of full back had to be entrusted to one who was unaccustomed to it, and in this the visi- tors were undoubtedly handicapped. Still, even had the Otley player not been injured, we fail to see how the Yorkshire men could have won. Their back division would not bear comparison with that of the other side. Only Lockwood and Dyson may be said to have given satisfaction, both playing well in their particular styles. Dyson is very quick on his feet, and when he gets away is not easily stopped. Bonsor did not come up to expec- tation by a long way, and was apparently playing on his great reputation. James Naylor did more genuine work. The forwards were a powerful lot, but they were slow, and once the ball came into the open their boasted superiority disappeared. One or two of them were guilty of shady tactics, which did not escape the notice of the spectators.

If one Lancastrian can be singled out for prain that man is Berry. No playersame in for so much notice throughout the afternoon. He is a half back of sterling merit, his only fault being that he is sometimes guilty of passing the ball to an antagonist. Although Bumby did well, he was overshadowed by the Tyldesley man. Flower was the only one of the three-quarters who did not do himself full justice. He did not field the ball smartly, and missed the pass several times. Marsh, on the other hand, was a splendid success. He was full of resource, and the way in which he dashed through the enemy was a treat to witness. He punted and followed up with wonderful smartness, and never hesitated to pass when collared. Valentine, too, came off, and had the satisfac- tion of gaining his first try against Yorkshire. Coop was all there at full back, and it may be safely said that he was never guilty of an error of judgment, whilst his kick- ing was excellent. The forwards surpassed themselves, and there was not a laggard amongst them. Strang's two tries were smart bits of work, and of the others Kent, Atkinson, Wilson, and Bothwell were conspicuous. Lancashire should now stand a great chance of the cham- pionship.
England v. Scotland is to be decided at Richmond this season, and North v. South at Blackheath.
ASSOCIATION.
We are informed that no match was played between Stockton Heath and Warrington Recs. as reported last week, Stockton Heath being engaged with Lysdale on that date.

The match between Warrington Association Club and Chester College was to have been played at Warrington, on Saturday, but was screched, the Arpley ground being more like a skating pond than a football field. This was a sad loss to the lovers of the club, as this was the best fixture on their cards. There is no doubt if the ground had been fit to play their funds would have had a good lift. Better luck next time. A little more sup- port to the club would make a lot of difference as they are a likely lot of fellows and will, perhaps, some day make a name for themselves.

All the League matches were brought off on Saturday, but the Rovers protested against the Condition of the ground at Everton. It was certainly dangerous, and to make matters worse a dense fog almost hid everything at times in its blackness. Everton won by three goals to one, and did by far the most pressing. Jardine, who has been transferred from Bootle, appeared for the Ever- tonians for the first time, and had a warm reception. The Liverpool club have now three capable goalkeepeis in Jardine, Angus, and Smalley.

Wolverhampton Wanderers are once more at the head of the League, not only as regards points, but also in the matter of average. They were too good for the North End, who again failed to score a single goal. They are terribly weak in attack, and with the single exception of Accrington, they have scored fewer goals than any other member of the League. This is counterbalanced some- what by the fact that less goals have been obtained against them, Everton coming next.

Notts ran clean away with Aston Villa at Trent Bridge, and now occupy the third place in the League table. They beat the Villans most decisively by seven goals to one, the Notts forwards playing in brilliant fashion. Derby County beat West Bromwich Albion for the second

div.head: POLITICAL CRISIS.
div.p: THE POLITICAL CRISIS.
MR. PARNELL'S MANIFESTO.

Mr. Parnell, in a manifesto to the Irish people, issued late on Friday night week, complains that the Liberal wirepullers have apparently destroyed the independenoe of the Irish party. He objects to Mr. Gladstone's claim to exercise a veto on their independence. Proposals were made in November last year, in conference between Mr. Gladstone and himself at Hawarden. These included the retention of the Irish members in the Imperial Par- liament, the settlement of the land difficulty, the control of the Irish constabulary, and the appointment of the judiciary. Mr. Gladstone, he says, contended for a re- duction of Irish representation from 103 to 32, the reser- vation of the settlement of the land question from the Irish legislature, and postponement of the two other pro- positions. Mr. Parnell objected to the reduction of re. , presentation until the Irish Parliament obtained control , of affairs, and to the disbandment of the Irish party until the foregoing important points were settled. After detailing his actions in Parliament on the Land Purchase Bill by arrangement with Mr. Morley, he adds that Mr. Morley suggested that he should accept the office of Chief Secretary for Ireland. Mr. Parnell objects to forfeit the independence of himself and party, and expresses belief that the Irish people, by supporting him, will not endanger the Home Rule cause, but that postponement would be preferable to the acceptance of an inadequate measure.
MR. GLADSTONE'S REPLY. THE IRISH LEADER CONTRADICTED.

Stn,—lt is no part of my duty to canvass the manifesto of Mr. Parnell, which I have read this morning, and I shall not apply to it a single epithet; for I am not his judge in any matter; and I believe myself to have shown in the matter of the Pigot Commission that I have no indisposition to do him justice. But the first portion of the document consists of a recital of propositions stated to have been made by me to him, and of objections entertained by him to those propositions. The Irish as well as the British public has a right to know whether I admit or deny

div.head: LAND PURCHASE BILL.
div.p: THE LAND PURCHASE BILL.

Mr. BALFOUR having moved the second reading of the Irish Land Purchase Bill, Mr. J. ELLis submitted an amendment to the effect that the House declined to pledge the credit of the country to the scheme pro- posed by the Bill, as being alike unsafe to the Imperial Exchequor, and unjust to thelrish occupier. Mr. GLADSTONE considered that, with the exception of the twenty year's limit, the changes introduced in the present Bill from that of last session were unimportant. He demurred, however, to the portion of the securities to be pledged being controlled tly a plebiscite of the ratepayers, but said it would be a great advantage to the Liberal party if this land question could be helped forward. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said Mr. Balfour's limitation would reduce the amount required under his proposition to one hundred millions, and therefore would be satisfactory to the House. He, however, advised the Government to withdraw the proposed omission of 20 years' maximum in the value of the property to be purchased, and ob- jected to allowing the State to become the landlord of Ireland. Mr. BALFourt said the total amount required to com- plete the system of land purchase would be 95 millions sterling, and if from this was deducted the thirty odd millions which it was proposed to allocate, with the cases in which landlords and tenants do not desire to sell or to purchase, a great impression would be made on the problem to be solved. He objected to any proposal giv- ing to a local authority control over individual transac- tions, and said that by land purchase alone could an end be put to agrarian discontent in Ireland. After further discussion, the debate was adjourned. The House adjourned at 12.10 a.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. _

div.head: IRISH LAND PURCHASE BILL.
div.p: THE IRISH LAND PURCHASE BILL.
Com

The adjourned debate on the amendmenti;Oposed by Mr. JOHN ELLIS to the second reading of the Purchase of Land and Congested Districts (Ireland) Bill was resumed by Mr. Canning, who supported the amendment. He considered that the price to be paid by the tenants was excessive. Sir John Colomb defended the Bill, though he could not regard it asa final settlement. Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT criticised the arguments of the previous speaker as to the value of dual ownership. Col. NoLax urged the Chief Secretary to include in the Bill provisions by which tenants might increase their holdings and also to give a definition of what constituted a congested district. Mr. SHAW LEFRVRE held that there was no evi- dence to prove that the Bill was generally acceptable to the Irish people. The debate was continued by Mr. W. P. Sinclair, Mr. Joicey, and Mr. Jesse Collings. Sir W. LAWSON opposed any pledging of the resources of the State to assist land purchase. Replying on the debate on behalf of the Government, the ATTORNEY-GENERAL for Ireland contended that no alternative scheme to the measure had been suggested, and that the Government measure would be safe to the taxpayer and bring pros- perity to Ireland. On a division being taken, the amend- ment of Mr. Ellis was rejected by 245 against 173, a majority of 72 in favour of the Government. Mr. WADDY objecting on the question that the Bill should be read a second time, Mr. W. H. SMITH moved the closure, which was carried by 242 to 172. The House then divided on the motion to read the Bill a second time, which was carried by 263 votes to 130, a majority of 138 for the Bill, which was afterwards read a second time, amid cheers. The whole of the Irish members present (with the exception of Mr. W. Macdonald, Dr. Tanner, and Mr. Flynn), voted with the Government in favour of the second reading. Mr. Gladstone retired from .the House immediately before the division. Mr. W. H. SMITH said he would put down the Com- mittee for Friday. The House then adjourned at five minutes past six o'clock. HODSE OF COMMONS--THURSDAY.
The Deputy Speaker (Mr. Courtney) took the chair at three o'clock. •

DISTRESS IN IRELAND.—In Committee Of Supply Mr. BALFOUR asked for a nominal sum to defray certain ex- penditure in connection with apprehended distress in Ireland. Ha said that in a considerable portion of the western district the failure of the potato crop had been very serious, and explained that a bill which he had introduced that day made provision for the granting of loans for the purchase of seed potatoed. Amongst the relief works suggested were land reclamation and afforesting, and it was pro- posed that all land reclaimed should be placed under the Congested Districts Board. Mr. John Morley held him-

self free to criticise the railway proposals at the proper time, but warmly approved of the seed potatoes scheme. After some discussion a resolution granting the vote was agreed to, and reported to the House. THE TITHES BILL.—On the order for going into Com- mittee on the Tithes Bill, Mi. F. S. STEVENSON moved that it be an instruction to the Committee that they should have power to provide for an equitable revision of tithes in accordance with the altered conditions of agri- culture. Sir M. Hicks-Beach protested against attempts being made to wreck the bill. Orba division the instruc- tion was rejected by 203 to 68, and the HGuse went into Committee pro forma, progress being immediately reported. In answer to the Deputy Speaker, Sir M. HICKS-BEACH said the Government proposed to proceed further with the bill on the 22nd January. hush RAILWAYS.—The House went into Committee on the Transfer of Railways (Ireland) Bill and agreed to 16 clauses. Mr. STOREY attempted to move an amendment to the effect that in no case should the price paid for the land required for railway purposes exceed 16 years' purchase of its net agricultural value, but he was ruled too late by the Chairman. A division:was challenged on the clause, which was agreed to by 224 to 22 amidst laughter. The other clauses were then agreed to. The bill was read a third time amid cheers. OTHER BILLS.—The transfer of Railways (Ireland) Bill passed through Committee, and was read a third time. The Private Bill (Scotland) Procedure Bill was postponed till after Christmas, and, the remaining orders run through, the House adjourned at half-past twelve.

SERIOUS OBJECTION, much less did he signify in whole, or in part, that they augured the proposal of a "measure which would not satisfy the aspirations of the Irish race." According to his present account, he received from me in the autumn of 1889, information of vital changes adverse to Ireland in our plans for Home Rule, and kept this information secret until in the end of November, 1890, and in connec- tion with a totally independent and personal matter he produces it to the world. 3. I deny, then, that I made the statements which his memory ascribes to me, or

ANYTHING SUBSTANTIALLY RESEMBLING THEM, either on the retention of the Irish tnembers,or on the set- tlement of the land or agrarian difficulty,. or on the con- trol of the constabulary, or on the appointment of the judiciary. As to land in particular, I am not conscious of having added anything to my public declarations, while as to county-eourt judges and resident magistrates, I made no suggestion whatever.

4. The conversation between us was strictly confiden- tial, and in my judgment, and as I understood in that of Mr. Parnell, to publish even a true account of it is to break the seal of confidence which alone renders political co-operation possible. 5. Every suggestion made by me was FROM WRITTEN MEMORANDA.

The whole purport of my conference was made known by me in the strictest confidence, when it had just taken place, to my colleagues in the Cabinet of 1886, and I assured them that in regard to none of them had Mr. Parnell raised any serious difficulty therewith. 6. Neither Mr. Parnell nor I myself was bound by this conversation to absolute and final acceptance of the pro- positions then canvassed, but during the year which has since elapsed I have never received from Mr. Parnell any intimation that he had altered his views regarding any of them. . . _

I have now done with the Hawarden conversation, and I conclude with THE FOLLOWING SIMPLE STATEMENTS. 1. I have always held in public, as well as in private, that the National party of Ireland ought to remain entirely. independent of the Liberal party of Great Britain.

2. It is our duty, and my duty in particular, conform- ably to the spirit of Grattan and O'Connell, to study all adjustments in the great matter of Home Rule which may tend to draw to our side mcderate and equitable opponents; but for me to propose any measure except such as Ireland could approve, on the lines already laid down, would be fatuity as regards myself, and treachery to the Irish nation, in whom, even by the side of Mr. Parnell, I may claim. to taken an interest. I remain, Sir, Your very obedient servant, W. E. GLADSTONE.
London, 29 Nov,

MR. MORLEY'S REPLY. Mr. Morley also replies to Mr Parnell's manifesto. Mr. Morley says he made no sort of attempt to fetter Mr. Parnell's action in the Land Purchase Bill. Mr. Parnell agreed with him in all their conversations that the bill ought to be opposed as otnittin,g the principle of local control, and for other reasons specified by him in kis speech of April 21st. The only question was as to the form of the motion for the rejection ,•,f the bill. Mr. Morley denies that he ever proposed the absorption of the Irish party into English politics, and says Mr. Parnell's account of what passed on the same occasion on the subject of evicted tenants on campaign estates is wholly incorrect.

div.head: LETTER FROM SIR W. HARCOURT.
div.p: LETTER FROM SIR W. HARCOURT.

A letter from Sir W. Harcourt contradicts the statement attributed to him by Mr. Parnell at the meeting of the Irish Parliamentary party on Monday, to the effect that neither now nor hereafter would he give any promise to any Irish party. Sir William explains that in his conver- sation with Mr. Justin McCarthy on the subject, he pointed out the unquestionable political fact that no party could ever hope to carry a scheme of Home Rule which had not the support of the Irish nation as declared by their representatives. Mr. Labouchere and Mr. James Stuart also write emphatically denying Mr. Parnell's as- sertion that they had been in treaty to put him out of his position in the Irish Parliamentary party.

div.head: MANIFESTO OF IRISH DELEGATES.
div.p: MANIFESTO OF IRISH DELEGATES.

The full text has been published of the manifesto of the Irish delegates in America on the present crisis. The document, which is signed by Messrs. Dillon, W. O'Brien, T. D. Sullivan, T. P. O'Connor, and Gill, while express- ing a strong sense of Mr. Parnell's matchless services to Ireland, declares that in his manifesto Mr. Parnell treats his party with cruel injustice. They repudiate as reck- less and unjust Mr. Parnell's attempt to fasten on Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Morley the responsibility for the pre- sent crisis. They declare that it is necessary for the good of Ireland that Mr. Parnell should retire from the leadership, and refuse to relinquish the hope that in face of the decisive action of the representatives of the Irish people, Mr. Parnell's sense of patriotism will withhold him from plunging her into the horrors of dissension which already in her history have so many times robbed her of liberty when it seemed within her grasp.

MEETINGS OF IRISH MEMBERS. STORMY PROCEEDINGS. The adjourned meeting of the Irish party to consider the question of Mr. Parnell's leadership took place on Monday in one.of the Committee-rooms of the House of Commons, and was of a stormy character. In the morn- ing Mr. Parnell met his supporters at the Westminster Palace Hotel. The proceedings there were kept private, the only informationViven to the reporters being con- veyed in a remark by the leader himself to the represen- tative of anllrish newspaper—" I will fight to the end." Mr. Parnell took the chair at the meeting of the party which commenced at half-past twelve and was attended by 74 members of Parliament. Half an hour was occu- pied in reading letters and telegrams, and then followed a long wrangle,as to the interpretation of th,e resolution which was before the last meeting when the adjourn.

ment to Monday was agreed upon. Tha Chairman held that this resolution, which was framed with the idea of giving him time to reconsider his position could not be withdrawn without the unanimous consent of those present, and, as this was not given, the only course open was to move amendments. Colonel Nolan then moved that the question of the chairmanship of the party should be postponed until members had had an opportunity of personally ascertaining the views of their con- stituents and until a meeting could be held sub- sequently in Dublin. This was seconded by Sir Joseph M'Kenna. Mr. Sexton strongly opposed the amendment. In his judgment the case was too urgent to adfnit of delay. He paid a warm tribute to the ser- vices of Mr. Parnell, but contended that no services, however great, entitled a leader to ruin his cause. Mr. J. Redmond followed with a defence of Mr. Parnell, and in his turn gave war to Mr. T. M. Healy, who urged that the claims of Ireland demanded Mr. Parnell's deposition. He repudiated the statement of Mr. Parnell that the in- dependence of a section of the party had been sapped by Liberal wirepullers,• and commented strongly on the course taken by the Irish leader after his interview at Hawarden. Mr. Parnell, after reminding Mr. Healy, and other opponents, that it was to him they owed their pre- sent position, said they were all agreed that they would not have such a bill as he averred was proposed at the Hawarden conference. Before they voted for his Jeposi- tion he wanted them to ask themselves whether they , were getting value for it. Were they sure that they would be able to do any better? If any of them could I say that they would be able to get anything better, "for [ God's sake let them say it, and I won't stand for a [ moment in the way." In conclusion he said he knew what Mr. Gladstone, Sir William Harcourt, or Mr. John [ Morley would do for them. None of the Liberal leaders ' were to be trusted unless the Irish members had trust in themselves. " I should like," Mr. Parnell added, "if you will permit me, to go with you until you are abso- lutely sure that Ireland and I can go no further." Mr. John O'Connor, Mr. T. O'llanlon, Mr. W. Redmond, Mr. P. Mahony, Dr. Kenny. Mr. J. Nolan, Mr. J. C. Flydn, and several other members afterwards addressed the meeting, which was eventually adjourned.

TUESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. ANOTHER ADJOURNMENT. At the adjourned meeting of the Irish Parliamentary party on Tuesday there was a repetition of the angry scenes by which Monday's long discussion was marked. The members assembled at noon, again under the chair- manship of Mr. Parnell, and the proceedings had only fairly commenced when it became apparent that there would be another protracted sitting. To begin with, much time was spent in a wrangle concerning a matter of relatively small importance, namely the nature and extent of the communications made to the delegates in America. It was alleged by members friendly to Mr. Parnell that in addition to telegrams forwarded in the name of the party and in accordance with the terms of an arrangement made between the two sections messages had been sent giving versions of the state of affairs which were misleading. The charge was denied on the other side, and then followed a series of scenes in which the uncompromising spirit actuating both sides was made clearly manifest. The debate on Colonel Nolan's amendment was resumed by Mr. O'Kelly, who supported Mr. Parnell. He urged in favour of the adoption of the amendment that it would give time to the country to think. He &dared that the power of the Liberal party to give Home Rule was limited by the power of the House of Lords, which was a barrier to all progress unless it was backed by the fear of revolution. Mr. Arthur O'Connor followed, and des- cribed Mr. Parnell as being now an impossible leader of his race. Mr. Richard Power, Mr. W. MacDonald, and Mr. Corbet supported, and Sir Thomas Esmonde opposed Mr. Parnell. Mr. Crilly and Mr. Kenny having spoken, Mr. J. F. X. O'Brien said that they had had very little of the leadership of Mr. Parnell in recent years. After the Divorce Court scandal he looked upon Mr. Parnell's con- tinued leadership as intolerable and a disgrace. A divi- sion was afterwards taken, in which 29 voted for the amendment and 44 against. The meeting was then ad- journed until next day. WEDNESDAY.—A FRESH MOVE. • - • • -•

At the adjourned meeting of the Irish Parliamentary party, on Wednesday, a proposal was made by Mr. Clancy which, it is believed, has materially altered the situation. Prior to this, however, a number of telegrams were read, including one from Father Humphreys, who %Pa 3uted at Tippgrary, declining to accept the prii ofTromeltUßY esclibeettiri-Ntr....Parnell's mani- festo. Mr. Sexton referred to an attack made upon him in one communication as ruffianly, and said that, not- withstanding such attacks, he should persist to the end in the course he had adopted. A telegram addressed to Mr. Condon stated that all the Smith-Barry tenants op- posed Mr. Parnell, whilst a message from Father Con- very,of Belfast, declared that the Nationalists of that city would have no leader but Mr. Parnell. Mr. Sexton said that if the Belfast branch of the National League took a view contrary to his own, he should resign his seat. Mr. Clancy then submitted his proposal, which was to the effect that, as a condition precedent to the further consideration of ate subject of the leader- ship, Mr. Gladstone and his lieutenants should be asked to give definite pledges with regard to their Home Rule proposals, particularly the points connected with the control of the constabulary i and the land ques- tion: It was clearly indicated that n the event of such pledges being given Mr. Parnell would consent to retire, "for a time," from the leadership. He declined, however, to make a distinct promise, and asked for time for further consideration, for which purpose the meeting was adjourned till next day. L'HURSDAY.—MR. PARNELL'S "TERMS." On Thursday Mr. Parnell placed before the meeting a resolution to which he asked them to pledge themselves, and which stated that no scheme for Home Rule would be satisfactory, which did not include the control of the constabulary and the settlement of the land question by an Irish Parliament. Assurances from the Liberal leaders on these points, satisfactory to the majority of the Irish party, he laid down as the condition of his retirement fro:n the leadership. After several speeches, in which a good deal of feeling was displayed, a resolution was arrived at to appoint representatives to wait upon the Liberal leaders on the understanding that Mr. Parnell would give way, if terms could be obtained such as were held by the majority to be acceptable. DECISION OF IRISH BISHOPS.
Iclple

The Standing Committee of the Archbishops and Bishops of the Roman Catholic Church in Ireland, meet- ing on Wednesday, at the residence of Archbishop Walsh in Dublin, declared without hesitation or doubt, and in the plainest possible terms, their unanimous judgment that whoever else is fitted to fill the highly responsible position of leader of the Irish people, Mr. Parnell de- cidedly is not. This judgment was given, not on poli- tical grounds, but on the circumstances revealed in the Divorce Court MR. PARNELL'S CHANGE OF FRONT. _ _

The "Daily News" says :—We have authority for publishing an extract from a letter containing impor- tant additional evidence respecting Mr. Parnell's inter- view with Mr. Gladstone, at Hawarden. The letter is from Mr. Edward Evans, who, as President of the Liver- pool Reform Club, took the chair at the dinner given to Mr. Parnell after he had visited Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Parnell stayed with Mr. Evans on the evening after his visit to Ha warden, and Mr. Evans says :—"ln the course of conversation (which was very free on Mr. Parnell's part), in answer to a question, he stated, or rather the purport of what he said was, that he was very much impressed with his visit to Mr. Gladstone, and at Mr. Gladstone's cordiality, but more than all with the thoroughness of his proposals with regard to Ireland, which really went further than he (Mr. Parnell) expected from any great English statesman, and that they meant a most satisfactory solution."

Ireland is divided in opinion as to the removal of Mr. Parnell; but throughout the rest of the kingdom the expression of opinion is almost universal in supporting Mr. Gladstone, and in condemning the conduct of the Irish leader.

div.head: SAD ICE ACCIDENT.
div.p: SAD ICE ACCIDENT.

LOSS OF FOUR LIVES. Four children, two girls and two boys, aged from twelve to fourteen years, were drowned on Sunday night at, Bloxwith, Walsall, owing to the breaking of the ice, upon which they were sliding. A fifth child escaped by scrambling to the bank.
MANCHESTER MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.

Vacancies having been caused in the Manchester City Council by the appointment of five aldermen for five of the wards recently added to the borough, the polling for five councillors took place on Saturday. In each ward the contest was for a Liberal seat, and when the votes had been counted it was ascertained that four Conserva- tives and one Liberal had been elected. The composition of the Council is now 45 Conservatives, 9 Liberal Unionists, and 49 Gladstonian Liberals.

LORD SALISBURY EN ROSSENDALE.

On Wednesday Lord Salisbury visited Waterfoot, in Lord Hartington's constituency, and, met with an en- thusiastic reception. In the afternoon he opened a new Conservative Club, which has been erected at a cost of £2,000. Addressing a crowded meeting in the club. he said the principal duty of the Conservative party in Rossendale at present was to support Lord Hartington• The alli Ince between the Liberal Unionists had been honourable to both sides, had been signally successful, had every prospect of enduring, and had been cemented without sacrifice of principle. At this moment its charac- ter was set in relief by the state of things in the other camp. A great meeting was held in the evening in the Myrtle Grove Mill, Waterfoot, and an address of welcome was presented to Lord Salisbury. Replying, the Prime Minis' ter said that only one subject occupied the minds of Ipoliticians. Mr. Parnell held the field. They all re- garded with deep interest the uprising in favour of domestic purity which the recent divorce proceedings had originated, but he wished the seventh command- ment had not eaten up all its brethren, and that similar denunciations had not followed upon the revelations of intimidations, murder, and outrage. It was an -extra- 'ordinary thing th2t. just before this trial came on, the leaders of the Opposition should have offered Mr. Parnell the responsible place of SecretarY for Ireland in a future Liberal Government. Without insinuating the slightest doubt of Mr. Glad- stone's honesty in denying the truth of Mr. Parnell'S version of the Hawarden interview, Unionists must be pardoned if they believed that some portion of the denial was coloured by the too brilliant hues of Mr. Gladstone ° imagination. Mr. Gladstone had the remedy in his own hands; if he told the country what he really did say that would dispose of the whole difficulty. Lord Salis- bury proceeded to discuss the points raised by Mr. Par- nell in his manifesto—the control of the police,landlegis- lation, and Irish representation at Westminster—and said Mr. Gladstone's policy of trust might lead them too far. If Home Rule did not produce separation at once, at least it would give the Irish Parliament a leverage with which to upset Mr. Gladstone's safeguards. As a matter of sentiment he would prefer the man who viao fighting for his life, to the crew whom:he had made and who were turning against him, and to whom Home Rule would give the entire control of the Irish population. n was the duty of conquerors to preserve order. That &VI we had hitherto failed to accomplish in Ireland, but un- der the straightforward policy of the Unionist Govern- ment success would be achieved.

THE DANGER OF BEING "GASSED."

Mr. W. Diggle, after the ordinary business at the Borough Police Court, on Monday, had been dis- posed of, complained to the magistrates with refe- rence to the deaths that have occurred at Golborne and Widnes through being " gassed " by the tanks. He said his object in appearing before their Wor- ships was to find out who was responsible for those acci- dents, for it was a great matter with the Coroner at Golborne to find out who was responsible for the acci- dent. He was of opinion that it was not Imlikely that the same thing would occur at the Intercepting Depots in Warrington. He had twice put the matter before the Sanitary Committee, but on one occasion there was no quorum, and on another date they said they had not any time to bother with the matter. He wished to get the magistrates' opinions as to who was responsible, perchance any such accidents occurred in Warrington. The Intercepting Depots were close to his house, and he was greatly annoyed at it, and he had found out that the nuisance arose from the defective plan of workings.—Alderman Davies : Do not go into all that Please. Tell us the facts of the present case. We do not care about the machinery because we do not understand it.—Mr. Diggle, coutinuing, said two men who worked at the Depots had been "gassed," and, had not assist- ance been at hand, very likely they would have lost their lives.—The Mayor said if Mr. Diggle's plans were considered by the Sanitary Committee to be likely to save life, hehad no doubt they would find time to go into the matter.—Mr. Diggle said he was quite prepared to put new plant down himself at his own risk.—The Mayor said if the Intercepting Depots were not removed, the Council would be able to apply to Mr. Diggle for his ex- perience and help, hut he thought that for the present it would be better to let the matter stand in abeyance.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The. fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Alder- man Harrison presided, and there were also present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Messrs. Blackhurst, Ratcliffe, Heaton, Davies, T. Jones, D. Jones, Jolley, Owen, Gill, Aukland, Hood- Wright, Ilibbert, Dignum, Clarke, W. Houghton Turton, .llather, Smith, Kilshall, Dobson ; J. d. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk.) CHRISTMAS DINNERS.
On the recommendation of the. House Committee the

80-aid approved of the inmates of the Workhouse having their usual Christmas dinner, with an allowance of one pint of beer for males, and half a pint for females, and coffee for those who preferred it. The Workhouse offi- cials are to be allowed for Christmas a turkey and four ducks. On the recommendation of the Schools Commit- tee, it was decided that the usual Christmas dinner be provided for the children and officers at the Padgate Schools. THE PROPOSED CRICKET GROUND AT PADGATE SCHOOLS. The Schools Committee reported that they had had under consideration the subject of setting apart a piece of ground for cricket, &c., as recommended by inspectors of the Loral Government Board, but after fully discussing the matter it was decided by seven votes to two not to do anything, the feeling of the Committee being that sufficient playground accommodation was already pro- vied.—The minutes were adopted. GIFTS OF NEWSPAPERS.

A gift of a parcel of newspapers to the inmates of the Workhouse from Mr. J. Buckton was acknowledged. THE WORKHOUSE CHAPLAINCY. The CLERK read a letter he had received from the Rev. S. Wilkinson chaplain of the Workhouse, in which he wrote "As I have always taken an interest in the poor pecple at the Workhouse if I had remained as chaplain it would have kept up a connection with Warrington where I have been so long, Allow me to thank you personally for all your kindness during the time we have been brother officers."—The CHAIRMAN said he had also received a communication from the Rev. S. Wilkinson in which that gentleman wrote "I must ask you to accept my resignation from December 24th. I hope this will allow you plenty of time to select my successor. Let me thank the Board for all their courtesy during ' the last 18 years."—On the motion of Mr. ELACKHURST seconded by Mr. Hot:Tomos the resignation was accepted.—Some discussion then took place as to a fresh appointment of chaplain.—Mr. HEATON suggested that it was desimble to consider whether the Roman Catholics, as well as other denominations, should not receive some payment for their services as well as the Church of England. He believed that plan had been adopted with regard to Roman Catholics at Padgate schools.—Mr. Hounwrox said the arrangement at Pad- gate was that payment should be made for seats.—Mr. DaviEsgaVe notice that when the appointment of chaplain was to be made he should move that in future a portion of the salary should be paid to the Roman Catholic clergymen for services in the workhouse.—Mr. RATCLIFFE supported this proposal.—The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON suggested that the appointment of chaplain should be deferred till the new vicar of St. Paul's was appointed. If there was any likelihood of the services being unper- formed in the meantime he should be very glad to give his services. (Hear, hear.)—The CLERK explained that the chaplain must by law be a clergyman of the Church of England,and he must have the consent of the bishop of the diocese. The present remuneration for the office was £BO a year. About one-third of the inmates were Roman Catholics and it Was found that Roman Catholic priests were very constant and earnest in their attention to the administration of the reli- gious duties, and in many Unions it was now the custom to give some renumeration to Roman Catholic priests in consideration of the services they rendered. He also mentioned that at Padgate £lO a year was given to the Roman Catholic Chapel and £lO to the Church of Eng- land.—Mr. RATCLIFFE mentioned several Unions where remuneration was given to Roman Catholic priests. —The CHAIRMAN next read a letter lie had received from Father

Feeny, of St. Alban's Catholic Church, who applied for the appointment as chaplain, and who pointed out that the inmates of the Workhouse had had the gratui- tous services of his Church since the year 1825, that these services had been rendered at the cost of much time and strength which could have been usefully spent in educa- tional and religious work outside the limits of the Work- house, that the increasing work thrown upon the priests by duties at the Workhouse was one of the reasons why the staff of St. Albans had been increased from two to three resident clergy Re (the Chairman) said Father Feeny was mistaken in thinking they could appoint a Roman Catholic to be chaplain, but he certainly thought. that as one-third of the inmates of the Workhouse were Roman Catholics - it would only be a just and equitable thing to pay Father Feeny a portion of the salary.—The Rev. E. C.E. CARLE- TON was of the same opinion as the chairman, but he snoke against cutting down the present salary of the Chaplain.—Some discussion then took place as to when the matter should be further dealt, with and eventually it has decided that it should come befere the members of the Finance Committee, which is composed of the whole Board, oh the 17th December. The Chairman, in the course of the discussion,•also mentioned that he had received an application from the 'Rev. I. Philips, of Orford.

TENDRIL The tender of Messrs. Relict and Cockerill, of Liver- pool, for work to be done at the tramp ward was accepted. The tender was £l4O, and it was stated to be the lowest received. The relief cases were then dealt with.

WATER AND GAS FOR PENKETH. Sir,—After reading your paragraph in last Saturday's paper on gas and water for Penketh, I would aSk 'Where is the movement on foot for it? I think the Corporation will find it at a very slow pace, as fax asTenketh is con- nerned. The *natter wasn't named at the November Township meeting, and very few ratepayers support it. Is it likely that owners of property, after paying,Slo to £2O, say, in sinking wells for their tenants (which is cer- tified to be good water) will pay for water when they get water for nothing? There might be a few Of the" Upper Ten " in favour of it; but I am certain there are none of the "Lower Five" to support it, sinless the landlordspay

for it. As far as gas goes, I will say nothing. I think the Cor- poration will find out that someonelas been' " gassing" them. Without a compulsory clause, I think the Curfew Bell would be beneficial in Penketb.—Yours, IE. CROSS.

div.p: Penketh, December 2.ndl 1890.

CRITICISM CRITICISED. Sir,—Your last issuecontained two notices, one of the Penketh Mutual Improvement Association, and the other the weekly meeting of the Wycliffe 'Young People's Society. Very suggestive the concurrence. of these two 'notices ; suggestive for one thing of imperfect reporting. Your Penketh correspondent neglected to give you what I consider to be the gist of the able,and interesting paper Mr. Gandy read, viz. that Count Tolstoi rejects the dogma of the Fall of Man and, I presume,y,with it the Ist of Genesis, but still calls and considers himself a Chris- tian! In this light I consider Tellatoi bua literary and logical phenomenon. I have hitherto 'thought that to destroy the foundation was to bring down the super- structure; that the doctrine of the Redemption was only logically complete when we accepted that of the Fall. This, however, by the way. Knowing the Penketh report to be thus incomplete,l suspected the integrity of that of Wycliffe. There I find illy estimable •friend Mr. John Dignum reading a paper on "Common ',Sense, versus Criticism;" very good. lam quite sure the absent critics got a very good mauting. But your reporter must have omitted to tell who it was -stood up 'for the poor down- trodden critics. Fair play demands that some one should have taken up the glove for thosevho, being ab- sent, could not defend themselves ;no that! infer that it was so ; that some more courageous meMber got up and said that, even if commonsense allowed the alteration of words and phrases in an important document to suit the fancy of the lecturer, common Justice and criticism would not ; that it Vasa very poor way of defending a book as divinely revealed to say that it•sar what it does not mean. By the wav, whenthe name of-Mr. Gladstone was mentioned as having squelched the Critics was that 4:)f Colonel Ingessoi referred to as having set him in a far back seat to play second fiddle ? It is a melancholy fact that, as in the days of decadence,of the ancient my- thologies, fables if poeticalty,mrpressedaremore accept- able to the herd than new truths however clearly and defineitly announced.—Yourslzc_, JOHN PEERS.

AND " COUNCILLOR HENRY .ROBERTS." Sir,—l should certainly not have troubled myself to , reply to Councillor Henry Roberts's lucubration which appeared in your issue of last Saturday, but for one con- , sidetation. He charges me with having inferentially accused ex-Sergeant Shaw, in ;my letter which appeared _ in your issue of the 22;nd ult., defendingthe Watch Cora- raitteee and the Chief Constable from themnjust asper- sion cast upon them by es-Sergeant Shaw and his ...admirers, of " shamming illness which I certainly -never meant to do. I take this opportunity of doing so, and, further, of expressing my regret, ;if I have con- veyed such an impression to the minds of any of your readers, for I have no reason to doubt that ex-Sergeant Shaw was really unfit, through illness., to ;discharge his duties, on every occasion in which he was absent on ; "sick leave," and I may say (by way of explanation) that an accidental omission of an interpolated line in the ; printer's copies of my draft letter would, if it had been ; inserted, have destroyed altogether an inference which Mr. Councillor Henry Roberts has taken so much pains to ,magnify. I may say, I did not copy the draft letter my- .self, nor had I the opportunity of seeing the copies before • they were sent to the Press. Otherwise I think 1 should *Lave detected the emission. ;With reference to all the rest of Mr. Roberta's letter, iitis but" Leather or Prunello," for it must be obvious to zany one (not blinded' by prejudice or passion) who „may :thank it worth while to compare the two, that it isco answer, whatever to mine, but is a studied evasion of tke facts, and incidents, as set forth by me, clearly showing that the treatment which ex-Sergeant Shaw received at the ;hands of the Watch Committee and Mr. Hunt, wet just,,onsiderate and indulgent is the extreme. But what Councillor Henry Roberts lacks in pewer to dispute, according te ,his ueual custom, he tries in the most repre- tensible manner to make up for it by puny insOlence. and awicorous abuse, but which, so far as I am concerned (corning from such a quarter), "passes by me as the idle wind, which Iregard not," as all his fulminations are as' potent as • the curses of the "Lord Cardinal," in the " Jackdaw of Rheims" for in spite of them, we are told, .0 Nobody seemed one penny the worse." Atiistpciat, I would conclude this letter, but while I have my pen on the paper I can hardly resist referring to -Ms calling me -t4 A miserable coward" (a delicasy and serenity of expression, which can hardly be too much admired.) And why? Because I did not say in the -Council Chainber, what I said in my letter when ex- Bergeant Shaw's 'matter was referred to. How many snore times; will it we necessary to tell Councillor Henry ;Roberts beforel2e gi:ae,psthe fact, that the conduct of the Watch Committee, intim management of the police force, is cot a debatable subject in the Council Chamber at all, and the mere mention of it,at the time to which he refers, :wasan irrelevancy, which precluded its discusdon. But, irrespective of that, I never intended to discuss it, because I knew perfectly welt, that the allegations made against -the Watch Committee;" and the Chief Constable. were .quite,uutrue, and that certain memters of the Council were trying to make political capital out of it, and I may .further say, that I should probably never have written my letter at all were it not that a respected member .of the Watch Committee, irritated at the gross mis- representation that had been made' called upon me a few ,days before its publication, with a letter he himself had written, which he left with me empowering me to rewrite, amend, and adapt it. as I theught fit, so as to meet the exigencies of the case, and I may say I did so far re-ieri te it, as to make it 'practically my own, so that although the publication of it was unpremeditated, Until within 4 low Asp provimly, conwillnr Henry

Roberts, with "logicality," purely ifs own, brands me, or lather tries to, with one of his el'Jgant expletives as a "Miserable Coward." (sic!) If I were a believer in the " "lirausmigration of souls" (which I am not) and could sc,e my way to form the ex- travagantly high estimate cf Cktuncillorßoberts'personal excellencies, which he does 'of himself, I should believe nothing less than that the Itcen-ntatetial part of "King Soloman" namely, his 'Nvisdem," had found a con- genial abiding place tKle the earthly int4gument of Councillor Henry P,ohotV.3. 'fiat 'cannot so etgard him. He rather forcibly rtominds me of "Mrs. Terser," in one of Gene nevelts (Adam Bede, Hink), who was being constantly "Ttblood.the wrong way" by an irtqa- ting, supercilious toung felloty, and not being ahlo to endure it any longtor, the worthy femake broke out into the following thapsody.:—" I don't wish that young man no harm, but I wish he was hatched over 'again, awl hatched proper." don't wish Councillor Henry Roberts" noraarm,” but.; I take leave to say, tkat if his gsbjection ta Mrs. Poyser's incubatory process could re- store him to us. purged from that acrebity of manner, bitterness et spirit, and unscrupulous Malevolence with which be is ever ready to assail friend or foe on the shortegTossible netice, and frequently from most ina- dequate causes, it would be a good thing in many ways for Cotncillor Heavy Roberts.—l am, Sir, yours, Sze., A MEMBER OF THE WATCH COMMITTEE.

div.head: LATCHFORD VACANCY.
div.p: THE LATCHFORD VACANCY.

As yet there' has been no formal declaration of a vacancy in Latchford ward, and consequently no uTfichil arrangements have been made as to the tilme for nontimations and the day of election. On Thurs- day evening a private meeting of the Conservatives of the 'Latchford ward was held in St. James' Schoolroom, to select a candidate in the Conserva- tiva interest to fill the vacancy. Alderman Harrison I presided. The names of five gentlemen were laid I before the meeting, and ultimately Mr. 'Linnmus Greening (son of the late Mr. Noah Greening?), wire manUfacturer, was selected. Mr. Greening'suddress willte found in our advertising columns.
"THE 'ALLEGED SWINDLING NIF A 'WARRINGTON FARMER.

At the Chester City Police Court on Thursdr.y, be- 'fore the 'Mayor (Alderman C. Brown) and other magistrates, a man named George Coates,(said to be a respectable farmer's son), appeared in the dock on a charge of conspiring to defraud at the last Chester Horse Fair. The case was that isa connection with one heard on Friday week at the City Police Court, 'where two men were charged for conspiring to defraud a man named Carter, a farmer, Burton- wood, near' Warrington, who it was was alleged was swindled out of £5O. The Mayor, after hearing evidence, remanded the prisoner, and said bail would be allowed as in the two previous cases, namely, prisoner in £5O and two sureties of £25 each.

The opening of the winter season of the Latch- ford Dramatic Society, took place mi Tuesday even- ing, in Christ Church Parish-room, under very favourable auspices. There was a Large and fashion-, able audience, and the performance was in aid of Christ Church schools The pieces that were staged were a comedy in one act, entitled "Sunset," by Jerome K. Jerome (founded on Lord Tennyson's second and longer poem of " therc isters"), and the well-known farce of "my turn next. The major portion of the acting in " Sunset," was alloted to Miss Dun, as Lois, and Miss A. L.Robinson, as Joan, and the dramatic ability which these young ladies displayed, evoked loud applause. Miss Reynolds excellently impersonated Aunt IDrusilla; Mr, Edelsten successfully represented Lawrence Leigh ; Mr. Finlay Dun admirably sustained the part ,of Azarial Stodd, and Mr. Rupert Crossley capitally rendered the part of Mr. Rivers (Lois's father). div.head: CHILDREN'S OPERETTA AT EARLESTOWN..
div.p: CHILDREN'S OPERETTA AT EARLESTOWN..

Mrs. Latimer, the tatented.musician, made her debut on Wednesday night, before an Earlestawn audience, in an entirely new character, showing at once that her abilities as a tutor were quite excep- tional. For some weeks past she had laboured hard in the task of preparing and training to a certain stan- dard of efficiency, a number of children of various ages, in the representation of a juvenile operetta. Her effort:: which to say the least, must have been attended with considerable anxiety, have been crov-ned with complete success, and no doubt this end has been greatly contri- buted to, by the aptitude of her pupils, who have entered heart and soul into the ,undertaking. Mrs. Latimer's juveniles appeared atthe Go-cperative Hall, or. Wednesday night, in the Operetta,- " Golden Hair and the rhree Bears," written by J. -,Aston Broad. The platform of the Hall had been completely transformed, and with the aid of foot-ti ' ghts -side wings, ke„, had the appearance of a theatre stage. The effect was excellent, the back ground cloth, representing a woodland scene, lording charm to' the surroundings. A large audiencetissembled in the hall, and loudly applauded the rising of the curtain., which disclosed to their view a forest glade, with a chorus of forest children, prettily attired in white, who sing in an excellent manner, &chorus describing who thespare and what they do. "Golden flair" (Miss Edith Southern) in a pleasing voice, tells in song, what a' " happy little maid" she is. She is ijoined by " Light- foot'', (Miss Agnes Needham) and ".Airy" (Miss Need- ham). On the exit of Lightfoot sisad Airy, the "Forest Queen*" (Miss Lewis) appears upon the scene, and sings of the,pleasures of the "Lovely dale,sweetivale of rest.' On the-call of the Queen, "Frailty" (Miss A. moiy_ neux) enters, and in pretty style "tails" ,the Queen. The Queen then tells Frailty of the home of "Bruin," who possesses jewels rich and rare, which she wishes to posseas,and asks for a maiden who is • proof against all harm. Trailty knowing of such, so informs the Queen. " Goldertflair, ' attired in black, is then broisght in by Frailty. "line Queen entreats" Golden flair' to stay with her; in the forest, promising to instalteras Princess. "Golden tHair," singing very sweetly ,and cteadily, accepts the honour, but the Bard" (Mr. James 'Lewis) in concealment, remarks in a rich voice, that " All things earthly pass away." The nextsceue shows the home of the ." three bears" who lived in the wood, and the story of whose doings delights theyoungsters. The big bear, was represented by Mr. ArthurLimond, "Mammy Muff" by Master H. A. Green, and "liny Cub" by Master Andy Liraond. In scene three,.the "Queen" and "Golden Hair" are discovered peated in the dale, and the Queen switly sings the story of the hidden treasures, "Golden Heir" undertakingthe task of finding them. "The Bard," on , the exit of tisnQuaen suddenly appears on the scene and startles "Golden Hair" but in a pleasing veice, though a trifle weak, reassures her, and advises her to rest on a grassy mound.. The bears then enter and are about to make Golden Hair"; captive, when" Will=o-the-Wisp '('ttiss Katie Cosilett) appsars and bids them begone. The -"Forest children" then enter, and cluster round" Golden( Hair" who is asleep,and sing a lullaby, joined by the. Xard." The scene again changes to the Bear's cottage.and scene five and last des,in:bes the search for " Golden flak," the condemnation by " Faithful " (Miss Rachel Thompson) of the Queen; her dethronement, the Ending of Golden Hair, andcoronation of the " Bard " as king, all ef which is prettily told in song. Too much praise cannot be bestowed on the,chorus singing which was really excellent, being tied with that sweetness which is so -refreshing when rendered (ay children. One or two of thasolos might have been improved, but on the wheleethey were rendered in -a manner quite in keep- ing with the age and surrounding of the performers. Thecastumes of the queen, the bard, and the bears, were quite realistic, and added greatly to the general effect. The operetta was repeated on Thursday evening when there was again a good audience, anti it was given with an equal measure of success.

—.a.... ate lett- Warrington in 1881, that, great as had been his activities in other directions, "they ate doubtless surpassed by his exertions on behalf of the religious institutions with which he has been connected. It is not too mudh to say that the present position of Dissent in Warrington, is due, in a large measure, to the efforts and example of Mr. Rigby. When, on coming to Warrington, he joined Wycliffe Church, the congregation was small, and the building in which it worshipped was an in- significant and inconvenient structure. But through the untiring efforts of Mr. Rigby, aided it is true, by many others who were roused into enthusiasm by his ardent spirit, the congregation multiplied and grew, increasing both in numbers and in wealth. The old chapel was soon found inadequate, and it was determined to erect the present handsome pile of buildings in Bewsey-st. The present church, built on the foundation of the old chapel, at a cost of some £12,000, will long remain as a monument to the religious zeal and activity of the distinguished townsman that is now leaving us. A. large, we be- lieve the largest, share of the financial responsibility of its erection rested with Mr. Rigby, and we are in- formed that he personally contributed £2,000 to the building fund. Mr. Rigby, moreover, has been a most devoted worker in the church. The Sunday school especially had won his sympathies. Both he and Mrs. Rigby have long been teachers in the school, and at the present time he is, we believe, oneof the superintendents. ' tin addition to this, he must be regarded as the founder of the Cockhedge Mission Chapel, Brick-st., a branch of the Wycliffe Church, which is now in a flourishing and prosperous condition. In 1869 MT. Rigby was placed on the roll of the borough and county magis- trates, and has, since his appointment, uniformly displayed, in his 'conduct on the Bench, a determin- ation to season sustice with merey. Mr. Rigby. it will thus be seen, is an eminently practical man. But the various activities we have mentioned, intense and lifelong as they have been, have not given rise in him, as such activities often do, to a contempt for things which are not practical. On the contrary, he is a man of taste and sentiment, one who takes a delight in antiquarian researches, in the productions of art, and in the masterpieces of literature. A. good many years ago he kbecame the occupier of Bruche Hall, one of the ,interesting old historic residences in this neigh- )bourhood. Previous to Mr. Rigby's tenancy, the Hall had been used as a school, and was left by its 'former tenant in such a condition as can easily be Imagined. Mr. Rigby at once set about to restore, complete, and decorate the ancient edifice. In particular, he added to it a part of the old ball, which had been used as an out-building, and fitted it up as a library, the result being the formation of one of the most charming and picturesque libraries that could be imagined. Since then it has been one of the hobbies of Mr. ' Rigi,y to stock it with the choicest volumes. and it was especially rich in illustrated books." _ _ . .

It was in consequence of declining liesitirthat, it. 1881, Mr. Rigby, in search of rest and change, left Warrington, and for some time after that hetresided at Mentone. In deference to his own strongly ex- pressed wishes, no publicq'eference was madeto his leaving, but a presentation was privately made to him of a magnificent album, containing the per- trs.tts,of a large number of the members of Wycliffe Church. After some time spent in travel, both on the continent and in England, Mr. Rigby settled in Chester, where he also took some part in pablic affairs. diuring the campaigns of 1885 and 1886.411 r. Rigby was chairman of Dr.'Foster's Election Com- mittee, remaining a staunch supporter of Mr. Glad- stone after the introduction of the Home Rule, scheme. He presided at most of the Liberal meet- ings held in the city, and had great hold npon his audiences, not by the number of 'his words, but la3r his pleasing, and convincing manner. Mr. Rigby, was often approached with a lie*/ to his beconanv a candidate for municipal honours in Chester, but he uniformly declined the invitation. He became identified with "}Torthgate Congregational Chureh .nd was appointed a deacon. He leaves a widow bet! -to children, He was twice Chairman of the Ches- hire County Union. Mr. Rigby, it may be mentioned, was one of the, founders of "The ,ExJaminer" along with Mr. John' Crosfield and the late Mr. George Crosfield and Mr. Mollinnies, and he tosk a great interest in its man- agement until it was ultimately sold ?to Messrs. Toulmin and Barker, prior to passing into the hands of the present firm.

THE EXAMINER, 9 SATURDAY DECEMBER 6, 1890. I . THE DEATH OF MR. SAMUEL RIGBY. - The death of Mr. Samuel Rigby removes another of the men who, in their time, has taken an active and honourable part in the public life of Warring- ton. Mr. Rigby's death took place on Tuesday at his residence Fern Rank, Liverpool-road, Chester. The sad event was in no way anticipated in Warrington, and its announcement was received with surprise as well as the =ow, wide-spread regret. Mr. Rigby had been performing his magisterial and other duties up to quite a recent date, On the 30th of September, he presided at the Occasional Court, Warrington, and more than a month later, on the 31st of October, he was on the bench at Liver- pool quarter Sessions, when there was Warrington case to be heard, namely, an appeal against the decision of the local magistrates to renew the license of the Royal Exchange public- house. About that time, however, he appears to have contracted an illness which confined him to his house till about a fortnight prior to his death when —indiscreetly,it must be said, considering the state . of his health and the kind of weather that prevailed, , —lie attermed a meeting at Manchester, of the Lan- cashire and Yorkshire Bank, of which he was a director. It was on this occasion that he caught the cold which orought about his fatal illness. Mr. Rigby was seventy-two years of age. His residence at Warrington began in 1860 when he succeeded the late Mr. Ward, as managing partner in Cockhedge Mills. These mills had previously been in the hands of Messrs. Hadfield and Frost, but after the retirement of Mr. Ward they were carried on under the firm of Messrs. Armitage and Rigby. It is largely due to Mr. Rigby that the business transacted at these mills has attained its present great dimensions. Under his management the place was re-built and re-organized, the most im- proved and best machinery being introduced. But the claims of Mr. Rigby to remembrance in Warrington are not merely, nor even mainly, based upon his action as a successful man of business. From the very ' beginning of his connection with Warrington he showed himself ready to give an earnest and active encouragement and support to every progressive and worthy movement. In'poli- tics, he was unswerving in his allegiance to Liberal principles, and for many years he was chairman of the Liberal party in Warrington. When, in 1868, the local Liberals decided to contest the borough, Mr. Rigby was the leader who was first invited to be- come the Liberal candidate. This was, however, a position he did not seek, and he declined the invitation, though at the same election he threw himself heart and soul, as chairman of the election commistee, into the work of secur- ing the return of Mr. Peter Rylands. After that election, he still continued at the head Of the local Liberals, and in 1880, 'be was again chairman of the election committee which achieved the triumphant return of the ,late Mr. McMinnies. Nor did the cause of progress and im- lorovement, in other than tho political sphere, ever lack his support. He was generous in his help to education, the People's College and W yeliffe Schools being particularly the objects of his concern. He was also a warm supporter of the cause of tempe- rance, and for many years he was chairman of the Warrington Savings Bank, and a vice-chairman of the Infirmary. To the last named institution he was a generous donor, and indeed liberal giving was one of the characteristics of the deceased gentle- man. It is computed by one who is in a position to form a fairly accurate opinion, that for-sotne years the benefactions of Mr. Rigby to religious and other noble objects in Warrington would not come far short of £l,OOO a year.. To Wycliffe ,Church alone, and its schools and societies, his gifts amounted to about ..£3OO a year. He was a decided and conscientious Congrega- tionalist, and his connection with Wycliffe is said to have begun on the very first Sunday which he passed in Warrington, and continued until the Institut. ...... in which he resided in the tow- -v «h.ira to the-Chairman pr0p0..,,,, hrouaht 17. Plough Road
late Mr. Rigby. He considered Mr. Rigby's self-denying life an object for all of theirrto emulate, and his political honesty worthy of that great party which he always adorned.

The CHAIRMAN, who spoke with much emotion, said they were called together that night to express their sympathy with a warm attached friend of Liberalism,not only in Warrington but throughout the world. He knew Mr. Rigby the whole of the time he was in Warrington. He recollected that Mr. Rigby had not been in residence amongst them very long when the American CiviL.War took place and brought with it ,the cotton famine. That gave Mr. Rigby an opportunity to show hie true charac- ter. He was engaged as they all knew, in cotton manu- facture in the town and employed a very large number of people, and, to his lasting credit let it be said, though they were losing money, the mill was never stopped. , He (the Chairman) would not say they worked full time, but employment was found for all of the people to an extent that was, perhaps, not seen in any other mill throughout Lancashire. (Hear, hear.) That was not the whole of the great work Mr. Rigby did at that time. For the purpose of affording relief to the indigent—and they might bear in mind that there was a great deal of distress in Warrington at that time—and not allowing it to appear to be what is commonly called charity, Mr. Rigby co-operated with himself and the present Lord. Winmarleigh in the establishment of a sewing school and found accomedation for that school in his own mill at Cockhedge, where female labour of every description in Warrington could find employment, and forthat employ- ment, which was an education at that time in the work they were doing, they was a given quantity of food provided. He might say a very great deal about Mr. Rigby, all of which was fresh to his mind, and so truly showed what the character of the man was, and how much he had at heart the well-being and the comfort of , his fellow creatures. (Hear, hear.) So far as Mr. Rigby's political life was concerned they all knew it as well as he (the Chairman) did. The first great work that he was connected with in Warrington, forthe Liberal party had been in a low condition up to that time, was in 1868, when there came a revival. When the time came for the selection of a candidate the man selected unani- mously in the first instance was Mr. Rigby, and Mr. 'Rigby at that time occupied such a pesition in Warring- ton that he( the Chairman) felt persuaded he would have been returned, by the earnest and hearty support of the Liberal party coupled with a feeling on the part of the more thinking Conservatives that lie was the best man in Warrington at that time to represent it in Parliament. (Hear, hear.) But Mr. Rigby's natural modesty, and perhaps some idea that his health was not equal to the work compelled him to decline the offer. Mr. Peter Rylands was then selected, and Mr. Rigby was the chairman of his committee and coached the election through from beginning to end, and when a petition had , been presewed Mr. Rigby was still the foremost man, both with with his money and his advice, in the work ' which was brought through successfully. (Hear, hear.) • As long as he remeined with them, Mr. Rigby was an ardent worker, and he naturally was the chairman of • the election committee when Mr. McMinnies was re- turned. Mr. Rigby had now done his work and gone to ' his account, and all he (the Chairman) could say was that he hoped they should all emulate his good example 1 in every way, so that when the time came it might be said of them that with the light that they had and the power and influence that they had they had done all they could and profited by Mr. Rigby's bright example. , (Applause.) He moved the following resolution "That the members of the Warrington Liberal Association have learned with the deepest sorrow of the death of Samuel Rigby, Esq., J.P. As president of this Association for many years he:devoted his time, abilities, and means most unsparingly to the promotion of the cause to which he was so sincerely attached. His noble personal charac- ter, his generous disposition and his genial courtesy greatly endeared him to all, and in the sad bereavement which bad befallen them we would offer to Mrs. Rigby and the other members of the family our heartfelt sym- pathy and condolence." (Applause.) Councillor 11. ROMELTS, in seconding the motion, said in the Sunday School Mr. Rigby was a brilliant example and in such a way as to make his face and his presence quite a gladness and a • jay to every one veho had the pleasure of being present under his superintendence and management. As a politician he was a magnificent ex- ample, always to the front and never wavering in any cause which he believed to be right. (Applause.) The resolution was also supported by Mr. S. Barlow, Councillor 'Flood and Mr. I. Heywood, and carrried unanimo___uslv. - A VO' ^l' thanks tifithe-CF'
... vote—at „ olpirt—i—lam proposed by Mr. C. J. Holmes and seconded by Councillor Beaman, brought the meeting to'a close. MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE,

Before the business of the County Police Court com- menced on Wednesday, Captain Withington said he wished to say a.few words, with deep regret, of the loss of Mr. Samuel Rigby. He had known the deceased gentleman for a great many years; he was twelve years his (Captain 'Withington's) junior as magistrate; but for over 21 years he had known him acting as a most pain-taking and conscientious magistrate on that Bench. . . . . . . .

Mr. BIICKTON (the desk), said he was at Mr. Rigby's house on Monday morning, and although he found him in a very serious state, he did not expect his end was so near. It was very sad indeed. Mr. H. T. FOILSRIVW, as a member of the legal proles- sloe, practising at Warrington, said he would like to say a few words with reference to the death of the deceased gentleman. He might-say that he had known Mr. Rigby for a considerable number of years,and had had business relations with him. 'He had always found him to be a most noble, and honourable man. As a magistrate he always executed justice and maintained truth. He was a kind and generous friend to the poor, and he was sure I by his death Warrington and other places had sustained an irreparable loss. "lie might also say that all of them deeply condoled with his widow in her bereavement.

At a Wycliffe Church meetingheld on Thursday a reso- lution was passed eavressing the most sincere regret and sorrow at the death of their old and valued friend Mr. Samuel Rigby and heart felt sympathy with Mrs. Rigby in her most grievouShereavement. div.p: BLACKPOOL SOUTH
PAVILION.

As will be seen from the prospectus in another column, a limited company has been formed for the porpose of erecting a promenade, pier, and landing stage,with pavilien,concert hall,open-air band kiosk, refreshment rooms, shops, Stc., at the South Shore, Blackpool. The capital is £60,000, in shares of Xi each. It is not estimated that more than 10s. per share will be called up ; and as Blackpool is still rapidly thriving, there is every prospect of the undertaking being successful. We give a view of the pavilion structure, which will be situated about 200 yards from the shore end of the pier. Encir- cling the main building will be a low colonnade, or verandah, which will afford ample shelter from sun or wind to a. large number of people. The band kiosk, with all necessary accommodation for open- air concerts, will be situated behind the pavilion at the extreme end of the pier structure; and here and there at intervals throughout the length of the pier promenade tastefully designed small kiesks or shelters will be provided.

div.head: SHOCIMiGfRAILWAY FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: SHOCIMiGfRAILWAY FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.

On Friday aifternoon, William Pickavanee, an uncle of the Rainford murderer, met with instan- taneous death under terrible circumstances at St. Helens. The deceased was both deaf and dumb, and re6ided at Preecot. He was 49 years of acre, and had been,empioyed as a labotrer by Messrs. F. and J. Goldsworth,. csntractors. His duty on Friday was to assist in unloading, a number of waggons of slag on a siding of the Ectieston branch line on the London and North-western ;Railway Company, near the stone yard of Couneallor W. 111. Foster, iron anerchant. Whilst returning from his ditmer about one .(clock Pickavance commenced to walk in the four-foot cif tthe two sets of rails in the siding. A wamber of coal waggons stood on one of the lines, and at that moment five waggons filled with slag were being.sh,unted on the otla-se set of rails. When near the deceased one of the slag waggons sud- denly leftthe rails, and before Pickavanee could escape he was knocked against,a coal waggon. 'As he fell to the ground a buffer "jammed" his head„ ,and the poor ;fellow's skull was terribly smashed. flis legs dropped ecross the rails in front of a,coal waggon started by the ,•esllision, and the wheels passed over his titighs, which :mere both broken. His-remains were removed to the .m)rtuary to await the inquest An inquest on the body of the deceased was held before Mr. S. Brlghouse,County ,Cotoner, at the Town Hall, cc Tuesday.—The Jury re- - turned a verdict of" Accidental death,' caused,either by sorna defect in the rails or the waggon, and recommended -that both the rails and the waggon should •becarefully inspected to ascertain where theifault arose.

It was stated that the defendant was ' employed asa salteake man, and for sow days after his appointmentattended to his duties. On the 17th Nay. A witness said that the total loss to the company was about £6. The defence was that the explosion was an accident, far which the defendant was not at all liable. After a long hearing, the Bench considered that the defendant had bow negli- gent, and made an order for the payment of £3.
