div.head: ST. HELENS GLASSIVORKERS AND THEIR SOCIETY.
div.p: ST. HELENS GLASSIVORKERS AND THEIR SOCIETY.

A preliminary meeting of glassworkers was held at the Churn ffaa, Tontine-st., on Saturday night, in connection with the proposed formation a a branch of the National Fedtration of Window-glass Workers. 'There was a moderate attendance. Mr. John Brawn, of &anderland, was present as a dele- gate, and gase an address on the importance of a strong trade organisation. He remarked that as many of the glassworkers of ISt. Helens did not wish to join the society of which Mr. P. J. King was pre- sident, he would advise them to form a local branch of the union he represented. It was ultimately decided to appoint a provisional committee, and to summon a full meeting of ghssworkers.—On Sunday afternoon a meet- ing of the glassworkers who had formed them- selves into a society under the auspices of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Um:on, was held iu the Public Hall, Hardshaw-st. There was a large attendance, and Mr. P. J. King, president, occupied the chair.—Mr. King stated that he had called them to- gether to lay down the lines upon which ther society should be governed, and to point out the necessity of repelling the attacks which were being made upon that organisation by outsiders. They were being recommended to serer their connection with the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, and to join some other organiasticn in another part of the country, but before the men took any such step as that he wanted them to be per- fectly certain as to the conditions upon which they did so. He (Mr. King) had succeeded in organising them, and had taken them in hand, and now that his labours were beginning to bear fruit outsiders Were anxious to come in and reap the harvest. He explained that the members of the society would in future have absolute control over its finances, and they would have the liberty of electlng their own committee. He asked them to take no notice of the claptrap and humbugging nonsense, about strangers, about aliens, and about men being unfit to lead them. Before he sanctioned their affiliation to the trades council. he wanted the Council to be composed of successful men. He did not want to be connected with a Trades Union that would contain as its leaders three men who forced men against their inclinations to return to work after 20 weeks' struggling without a atingle concession. (Applause.) The meeting was ultim- ately adjourned for a fortnight.

TEMPERANCE LECTURE. —On Tuesday a temperance lecture on " Popular Errors—Practical Truths," was given by Mr. George Blacklock, of London, in the new Assembly Hall, Kemble-st., Prescot, before a very large assembly which from appearance would number 1,000. The Rev. Harry Mitchell, vicar of Prescot, presided. The lecture was listened to with much attention and was fre• queutly applauded.

Thus ConaparT has been formed for the purpose of erecting and warking a Promenade Pier and Landing ,Stage, with pavdieu eoncertarall, opea-air band kiosk, refreshment rooms, shops, .and lavatories thereon, at South Shore. Bladkpool. Bleat:pool undoubtedly ranks amoegst the fleet and fore- most wee-teeing places of Great Britain, probably none being better known or -situated mere advantageously as regards fine open coast, refreshitegauddavigorating breezes, and magnifi- cent stretch of -bead:. The desolepment.af Illackpool hes been singularly rapid. In 1831 the aumber of its inhabitants ,was below 1.600; in 1861 its people weressmnputedat 3,500, team which time for- ward its progress is particularly uoticeable, last year the resident popsaation of Bleekpost being estimated at no less than 23,000 persons. In the summer months the average daily population is vari- ouely estimated at 100,000 to 200,000 people, while the awe- gate number of visitors during the season is calculated as being considerably over 1,000,000, a very large proportion of whom stay at South Shore. The existing North Pier was erected in the year 1862. Six years afterwards, Blackpool had so far exteuried as to justify' the erection of a second pier, about half-a-mile further south —the present South Jetty—which was opened in 1868. Since that time the extension of the town has been almost entirely southward, to fact, so rapid has been the growth of the South Shoreihat to-day there is a continuous mile of houses between the South Jetty and the southerly end of the Promenade. Judging from the experience of the last few years there is every reason to believe that within the immediate future South Shore will become the more important part of Black- pool, and will extend right away to St. Anne's-on-the-Sea. Building operations continue to be extensively carried on there, and every available plot of land is readily acquired for building purposes. The populatto of South Shore is entirely due to its natural advantages, combined with easy access from all parts ; it has not as yet any place of amusement, or any public building suitable for enterdainments. In order, therefore, to meet the requirements of visitors in this respect, it had been decided to combine with the %%tended Pier a large and handsome pavilion, particularly adapted for concerts and other entertainments of similar nature • this pavilion will be capable of seating with comfort an audience of over 1,800 people. A grand organ in the interior will form a leading featuree-an aquisition which will enable the better rendering of choral music, an always successful and agreeable attraction—and, in addition, will make the pavilion available for organ recitals, which have become so popular. Open tenders for the erection and con- struction of the Pier and Pavilion, lee., will be publicly advertised for. Having regard to the fact of the financial success of the two existing piers in Blackpooland, taking into consideration the many advantages which this Company's Pier will possess. there is every reason to anticipate that the profits will be sufficient to pay excellent dividends and leave a handsome surplus for reserve fund and founders' apportionment. The venture is bound to be a big financial suceess, for it will practically have a clear field, and cannot be regarded as, in any sense, clashing or competing with any other resort in the town."—Vide" Blackpool Herald," Friday, October 17th, 1890. The surplus net profits of the year are to belong as to one- half, to the holders of founders' shares pro rata, according to the number of such shares held by them ; and as to the other half, to the holders of ordinary shares. The directors have full power to appropriate to a reserve fund such sum as they may deem desirable before declaring a dividend. the founders will pay all legal-, advertising, and ether charges, except brokerage, incidental to the formation and registration of the Company up to the first allotment of shares.
